utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone here in the courtroom. Ten months after the Prosecution started its case, the Defence under Rule 98 bis is now in a situation to give its own analysis, its own view, of the evidence adduced so far and to state itself views as to what it considered to have been proved and what has not been proved regarding the acts that the accused have been charged with, and in particular of course General Lazarevic. In the indictment, the Prosecution has charged my client, General Lazarevic, and the other co-accused in this case the commission of crimes listed in Counts 1 through 5 of the indictment and then these counts were specified in greater detail in paragraphs 70 through 77 of the indictment. For the crimes listed in Counts 1 through 5 of the indictment, it is the Prosecution's view that the accused General Lazarevic is responsible under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. In the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution offered evidence that he -- that it intended to call with regard to each of the accused in the course of its case, that this evidence was supposed to support the allegations in the indictment. General Lazarevic's Defence finds that the larger portion of the evidence that the Prosecution based its indictment on has not been called at all. In fact, a major portion of the evidence has not been admitted and the evidence that was adduced before this Trial Chamber is such that it does not support the allegations in the indictment, in particular, the evidence that is supposed to support individual criminal responsibility of General Lazarevic. That is why in the course of our oral arguments we will focus on the evidence that pertains to the individual criminal responsibility of our client called by the Prosecution in the course of its case. We would like to add here very briefly that in the spirit of Rule 98 bis, in our analysis of the evidence tendered and admitted into the record, we would like to make our contribution and assist the Trial Chamber to make a decision that would reflect the interests of justice and the demands for a fair and expeditious and economical trial. As my colleagues have noted before, in our view an economical trial is a trial where we do not have to challenge the -- what the Prosecution has failed to prove. We will first say something about General Lazarevic's responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. We are convinced that, in its case, the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt General Lazarevic's responsible for the crimes listed in the indictment on the basis of his responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. The Prosecution alleges that each of the accused, including our client, is responsible under Article 7(1) for his contribution to the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise, whose purpose it was to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo by criminal means, in order to ensure further Serbian control over the province. The Defence contends that even though the Prosecution is relying both on the so-called basic concept of the JCE and, alternatively, on the so-called broader concept of the JCE, has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that all the requisite elements established by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal in fact exist for any of those two concepts. We would first like to note to you, Your Honours, that the Prosecution failed to prove the existence of any plan or design to change the ethnic balance in Kosovo by criminal means, and in particular it has failed to prove that this plan came into existence at the latest in October 1998 and the Prosecution failed to prove the existence of any plan aimed against the civilian Albanian population. When the Defence says that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt the existence of such a plan, it relies on the evidence provided by several Prosecution witnesses whose -- and this evidence, to say the least, brings into doubt such allegations made by the Prosecution. So to give you an example. The first Prosecution witness, high-ranking OSCE official Sandra Mitchell, claims in her testimony that until the 20th of March, 1999, she was the acting member of the OSCE mission in Kosovo and that the plan for monitoring the refugees was made only on the 22nd of March, 1999, and the reason for this, as she says, is because they did not have a refugee problem before that. That's at page 588 of the transcript, lines 1 through 3. It is quite obvious that when the OSCE mission and the Kosovo Verification Mission left the province of Kosovo and when the -- when NATO announced openly that within a few hours it would start an intensive air-strike campaign against the FRY, it was quite inevitable for the civilian population to leave the province en masse. In light of the fact that until that moment there had been no major movements of population out of the borders of the FRY - or at least the Prosecution failed to adduce any evidence to that effect - any reasonable trier of fact would be able to see the causal link between the impending NATO air-strikes and a possible ground offensive and the departure of the civilians from the territory of Kosovo. After all, there was a large movement or exodus of people at that moment in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia. The Defence does not challenge the claim that within the province of Kosovo there were some instances of internal displacement of civilian population, but what it does challenge is the claim that such transfers of population were forcible, caused by expulsions or any other form of duress exercised or forced -- exercised by the forces of the FRY and Serbia. The Prosecution has failed to prove that the internal displacement of Albanian civilians within the province of Kosovo were a result of violent activities on the part of the FRY and Serbian forces targeting the civilian population with the aim of implementing the above-mentioned plan. So apart from the cases of legitimate transfer of population caused by combat activities, there is a lot of evidence establishing the existence of a KLA plan to ascribe such transfers to alleged violent activities of the FRY and Serbia and we will now list some of the major evidence to support this claim. One of the key Prosecution witnesses, the Chief of Main Staff of the KLA, Bislim Zyrapi, quite unequivocally stated in his evidence that the civilian Albanian population had withdrawn together with the KLA and that this had been the usual practice, purportedly for security reasons because of the risks inherent in the combat between the KLA and the Serbian forces. That's at pages 5991, lines 17 through 25; page 5992, lines 1 through 15; page 5997; and 5998, lines 1 through 23 of the transcript. It is the Defence's view - and it seems to us that the honourable Trial Chamber has also noted this - that it is quite obvious that the risk for the civilian population is far greater if it is moving together with the KLA troops, that's at page 6003, lines 7 through 23. So these are the responses to questions asked by the Trial Chamber. Furthermore, a specific order issued by Bislim Zyrapi on the 1st of April, 1999, is in the record in this case. In his capacity as Chief of Main Staff of the KLA he is ordering the movement of Albanian civilians from the village of Belanica. That's Prosecution Exhibit P2457. Another major Prosecution witness, deputy head of mission of the Kosovo Verification Mission, General Drewienkiewicz, in his evidence said something about the Prosecution Exhibit P680, where it says that in the Djeneral Jankovic region the KLA ordered the civilian population to move out, which they actually did, by the 27th of February, 1999, and in his view this document was accurate and credible. Jan Kickert, in his evidence -- I have to apologise. Let me just give you a reference for the previous quote. That's at page 7932, lines 2 through 21. Jan Kickert gives evidence along the same lines. In the relevant period he was the secretary of the Austrian embassy in Belgrade. He also established a direct link between the KLA and the internal displacements of the population. That's at page 11222, lines 1 through 17. The documentary evidence and the oral evidence of major Prosecution witnesses lead us to say that there is reasonable doubt, to say the least, about the existence of a plan to internally displace or deport the Albanian civilian population by violent and criminal means. If the Trial Chamber, despite the evidence referred to above, should find that the Prosecution did prove beyond reasonable doubt the existence of such a plan, then we say that the Prosecution still failed to prove that the Yugoslav Army and General Lazarevic in particular had any knowledge of such a plan and that he participated in it consciously and deliberately. A number of Prosecution witnesses, including high-ranking foreign officials of the OSCE and the Kosovo Verification Mission, support the Defence argument regarding those allegations. Because of the nature of the 98 bis motion, what it should do, we will now move on to say something about some of the evidence that has been adduced. Colonel Crosland, the representative of the UK-KDOM, spoke about his personal experience and his visits to the VJ barracks throughout Kosovo from October 1998 onwards, and he says that the VJ carried out its regular tasks and that their mission had no objections. That's at page 9955, lines 3 through 10. Furthermore, Prosecution witness General Maisonneuve, the head of the region centre 1 of the Kosovo Verification Mission that covered the municipalities of Prizren, Suva Reka, and Orahovac, when he speaks about the isolated incident at the Pastrik Mountain on the 14th of December, 1998, and also when he speaks about the conduct of the VJ troops and the troops of the 549 Motorised Brigade troops in general terms, because this unit was active in his centre -- in the zone that was covered by his centre, stresses that the VJ's conduct was humane and professional. He notes that the VJ carried out its operations in a professional manner and did not enter into the villages at all. That's at pages 11131, lines 8 through 24; 11132 [Realtime transcript read in error "11134"], lines 5 through 25; and 11133 [Realtime transcript read in error "111"], line 1. Your Honours, there is an error in the transcript. It's not 1134 but 1132 and after that 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And excuse me, please, but just it might be an error in the transcript, it's pages 11131, lines 8 to 24, 11132, lines 4 to 25, and 11133, line 1. This witness also goes on to say on page 11152, lines 5 to 18, that combat groups of the VJ in Kosovo will be deployed in compliance with the October agreement and that he was at liberty to visit all of these units and had permission to do so. Witness General Klaus Naumann, the chair of the NATO military committee, also spoke about the professional approach of the VJ in activities outside of barracks as well as its professional and correct cooperation with the OSCE mission in the period from January to February 1999. Page 8357, lines 12 to 15. Furthermore, Witness Colonel Richard Ciaglinski, a member of the Kosovo Verification Mission, also evaluated the behaviour of the Army of Yugoslavia in Kosovo, both in specific incidents and in general. As regards the specific incident on the Pristina-Podujevo road when a colonel of the VJ was killed in an ambush, and this witness was questioned about this incident, both during direct examination, cross-examination, and re-direct, stated quite decidedly that he was a witness to this operation from the beginning to end, that the VJ carried out this operation in a professional manner, that he saw nothing irregular, and that there was no retribution, destruction or killing. Your Honours, I can offer you a number of references for what I have just said as follows. Page 6847, lines 13 to 25; page 6848, lines 1 to 4; page 6908, lines 19 to 23; page 6927, lines 17 to 25; page 6928, lines 1 to 2; and finally Exhibit P2488, page 9, paragraph 4. This same witness also spoke about his visit to VJ units in Junik on the 24th of January, 1999, when he had occasion to talk, as he himself testified before this Court, with local ethnic Albanians who told him on that occasion that they did not have any problems whatsoever with members of the VJ. That's on page 6896, lines 6 to 13. As regards his general assessment of the behaviour of the VJ, this witness added that he had occasion to see numerous reports drawn up by members of his mission and that there were no complaints about the behaviour of the VJ in any of them. That's page 6894, lines 23 to 25; page 6895, lines 1 to 2. We cannot but observe that Witness Ciaglinski, when referring to the actions of the VJ in the border belt, asserted that these actions also were carried out by the VJ in a correct manner and without any problems. That's page 6910, lines 10 to 22. 10 to 22, Your Honours. And finally, in the transcript on pages 6929, lines 18 to 25; and page 6930, lines 1 to 3, Witness Ciaglinski, especially emphasised that the VJ up to the moment when he left Kosovo behaved correctly and did not use undue force or excessive force. Prosecution Witness K79, in his testimony, first on page 9721, line 12 to 20, mentioned a specific incident in the village of Ljubizda where he was an eye-witness who saw the VJ return civilians to their homes, and then in his further testimony on page 9728, lines 7 to 13, he confirmed that members of the VJ in his area behaved professionally in every respect. This same witness during re-direct, when asked by the Prosecutor whether he based his knowledge about the arrest of VJ soldiers on an example that he saw replied that apart from this one incident he had also heard of others. The Defence -- I do apologise, Your Honours. The reference for what I have just said is page 9729, lines 5 to 10. The Defence cannot but analyse the testimony of Shaun Byrnes, the chief of the US-KDOM when he spoke about the cooperation of members of the VJ with the KDOM mission and assessed it as a exceptionally professional and positive. Page 12144, lines 5 to 25. The Defence wishes to point out that this witness, when testifying before this Tribunal and referring to the period from August to September 1998, concluded quite clearly that the VJ did not participate in the torching of villages, destruction of crops, killing of livestock, or similar crimes. Page 12150, lines 5 to 12. Furthermore, Witness Shaun Byrnes, referring to a later period of time, that is, the period throughout 1999, also pointed out that he never saw the VJ involved in the perpetration of any such crimes, nor did any of his teams ever report any involvement by the VJ in the perpetration of such crimes. That's page 12150, lines 15 to 17. Witness Shaun Byrnes goes on to say in his testimony that he learned from Kosovo Albanians working in his mission and from Albanians belonging to the Kosovo political elite and who were refugees from Kosovo, and he learned this later on that the VJ, even after NATO air-strikes began, treated them with respect. He mentioned a specific incident where the VJ intervened to save the lives of two Kosovo Albanians who were employed by the US-KDOM. That's on page 12199, lines 18 to 25. The Defence is convinced that the Prosecution will attempt to counter this testimony with other views of the role of VJ in the relevant period, but the quantity and probative value of this testimony is such that no reasonable trier of fact could reach the conclusion that it has been proved by the Prosecution beyond reasonable doubt that the VJ participated in the alleged joint criminal enterprise. The Defence also submits that the Prosecution failed to prove in its case that General Lazarevic was a member of the alleged JCE and that by his actions he consciously contributed to the implementation of such a plan or enterprise, or that he had an intent either by action or omission to contribute to the implementation of such a plan. The Prosecution has failed to prove that General Lazarevic was aware that there was an attack aimed at the civilian population and that his actions were an integral part of that attack. As it has remained unproved that General Lazarevic was aware of the existence of a JCE aimed at the civilian population or that he had any intent of participating in such a plan, he cannot be held responsible for those actions concerning which no agreement has been reached in a JCE and which might be a natural and predictable consequence of a possible plan so that there is no mens rea in this case, which is -- which must be shown to exist in order to make a finding of responsibility under the third basis of JCE. We now wish, on the basis of certain examples from the evidence, to show that General Lazarevic neither ordered nor planned nor instigated anyone to commit a crime. There is also not a single piece of evidence that would indicate beyond reasonable doubt that the accused General Lazarevic aided and abetted the perpetration of crimes, those crimes with which he's charged in Counts 1 to 5 of the indictment. It has not been proved in relation to any of these modes of participation in a JCE that the accused General Lazarevic had either the actus reus or the mens rea required. The allegations, or rather, the statements in the indictment, in paragraph 309 in the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, that General Lazarevic, starting from 1999 up to the 10th of June was the commander of the Pristina Corps are correct and there is no doubt about this. It is also not in dispute -- in other words, the fact that he was the commander of the Pristina Corps is not in dispute. What is in dispute is that based on this fact alone his responsibility can be established. This fact on its own is not sufficient to make a finding of criminal responsibility, either under Article 7(1) or Article 7(3) of the Statute. In its pre-trial brief the Prosecution suggests that General Lazarevic contributed to the implementation of the plan through his role in the Joint Command, but the Prosecution has not succeeded in proving what the so-called Joint Command actually was. The Defence asserts and submits that General Lazarevic was never a member of the alleged Joint Command, and this is based on evidence tendered by the Prosecution in this case. Thus, Exhibit P1468, which are the minutes from meetings of the so-called Joint Command, starting from the 22nd of July, 1998, until the 30th of October, 1998, and these minutes are from more than 60 meetings, shows when these minutes are analysed that it can clearly be concluded that there was no attack, no plan, no action aimed against the civilian population. When you look at one of the minutes from these meetings dated the 23rd of August, 1998, it can be clearly concluded that General Lazarevic was not a member of the so-called Joint Command because you can read who is present and who is absent and then it is added "and General Lazarevic." So a logic, or rather, "Colonel Lazarevic." It can clearly be concluded from this that General Lazarevic attended the meeting but was not a member of any sort of command. And we submit that it was not a command actually in the true sense of the word. General Lazarevic up to January 1999 was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps and he spent this time at the forward command post in Djakovica. Neither in 1998 nor in the following year, 1999, when he became the commander of the Pristina Corps did he ever attend meetings of high-ranking political, military, or security officials in Belgrade where the alleged joint criminal enterprise is said to have come into existence and was implemented through the Joint Command for Kosovo. An analysis of Exhibit P2166 leads to this conclusion quite clearly and unambiguously. The Prosecution simply cannot claim the opposite because there is not a single piece of evidence to support this. Numerous witnesses here have been asked whether General Lazarevic was a member of some sort of Joint Command and not a single one said that he was. The Defence contends that the so-called Joint Command, regardless of its title, did not have any command function and it did not in any way violate the usual and legal chain of command, both in the MUP and in the VJ. After all, Prosecution Witness Ljubinko Cvetic when asked explicitly by the Presiding Judge whether after the establishment of the Joint Command, the chain of command, as it was envisaged by law, continued to exist in the VJ and in MUP, he replied quite explicitly and clearly that it did continue to exist. That's at page 8123, lines 6 to 12. Another piece of evidence to support this is the fact that there was no chain of command within the Joint Command itself, that there was no commander, no chief of staff, no other organ that must exist in any command and the Joint Command itself did not have its command post; there was no usual reporting system established that has to exist where operative or combat reports must be submitted. All those facts not only undermine the Prosecution argument that there was such a thing as a Joint Command, but, in fact, support the claims by the Defence that it had no command function and that this was not, in fact, a body where the powers and authorities of military police and political structures came together. The Prosecution claims that General Lazarevic participated in the joint criminal enterprise primarily by using his position to plan and order operations in which crimes were committed, crimes that he's charged with in the indictment, and that he contributed to this enterprise with intent to commit those crimes. The Prosecution has failed to prove this allegation beyond reasonable doubt and for a very simple reason: It failed to present any order issued by General Lazarevic in his capacity as the PRK commander that would support this allegation. If we want to analyse the orders that General Lazarevic issued as the commander of the Pristina Corps admitted into evidence in this case, it is possible to make an unequivocal and clear conclusion that their purpose is solely to engage PRK units in combat against the KLA and to protect personnel against NATO air-strikes. In his order dated the 25th of May, 1999, admitted into evidence as P2014 - one of the key Prosecution witnesses commented and evaluated this order, this was General Vasiljevic - General Lazarevic orders, or rather, prohibits uncontrolled entry of the troops into inhabited areas, prohibits any plunder of property - that's under paragraph 9. And in paragraph 11, moral and psychological support, he explicitly orders that civilian population is to be treated in a proper and humane manner, and that the provisions of international law of war are to be respected consistently in all situations. So this is what is -- what General Lazarevic says in his order, an order that was tendered into evidence by the Prosecution in this case. We have a same situation with an order issued by General Lazarevic as the PRK commander, admitted into evidence as P2029, on the engagement of the Pristina Corps forces. In addition to regular combat tasks, he specifically orders his units to prevent plunder, theft, and all other forms of crime and war profiteering and to protect the population against criminal activities and robbery. General Lazarevic demands from his subordinate units to identify and apprehend the perpetrators quickly and efficiently and to do the same to all those who are responsible for any negative kinds of conduct, and the military court would then take the appropriate measures provided by the law. The Prosecution asked its witness General Aleksandar Vasiljevic to analyse an order issued by General Lazarevic as the commander of the Pristina Corps, this is the order admitted into evidence as P2014, and this witness said that this order was a typical document drafted in a very precise and professional manner by the PRK command and that this was a high-quality order. That's at page 8732, lines 17 and 18, and at page 8734, lines 13 and 14. In order to help the Chamber create a clear picture of those Defence arguments, we also have to note that the subordinate units, when they implemented the orders issued to them by the superior command, the Pristina Corps command, and General Lazarevic focused in particular on the protection of civilian population. Just to give you an example, you can find this in Exhibits 5D86 and 5D87. In those orders, the commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion issues an order specifying that platoon and company commanders are responsible for the prevention of plunder, terror, and similar crimes and that civilian population is to be treated in a professional manner and that any unnecessary destruction of buildings is to be avoided. Special emphasis is placed on the protection of civilians and that particular care must be taken of children and the elderly. One should also note the orders issued by the commander of the Pristina Military District, 5D32, dated the 20th of April, 1999; and 5D35 dated the 24th of April, 1999. In those orders, special focus is placed on the protection of civilian population. There is a prohibition against any wilful acts aimed at a civilian population and the prevention of any movements or transfers of the civilian population, except when the civilian population is at risk because of combat or NATO air-strikes. If there is any threat to the civilian population, the order stipulates that they are to be evacuated and provisionally put in a provisional location. The commander of the Pristina Military District Zlatomir Pesic testified before this Trial Chamber as a Prosecution witness, and he confirmed in a clear and unequivocal manner that from the time when he was resubordinated to the PRK command in mid-April 1999, he never received any oral or written order from General Lazarevic that would be contrary to the law or to the basic rules of engagement of the VJ. That's at page 7267, lines 4 to 13. We consider on the basis of all that we have stated above that the Prosecution has failed to proffer any evidence to support the allegation that General Lazarevic contributed to the joint criminal enterprise by ordering and planning, and the Prosecution in particular failed to prove that he had the intent to commit any such crimes. The Defence does not rule out the possibility that in some operations and in combat with the KLA and in the course of defence against NATO air-strikes, some acts were committed that were contrary to the orders and those acts resulted in criminal offences, but such cases - it is our contention - can be considered individual incidents and accidental consequences and cannot be considered as efforts to implement a plan of which my client was purportedly aware and purportedly had the intent to actually implement it. We have to add here that whenever General Lazarevic learned about any such incidents, he reacted by filing criminal reports in order to prosecute any persons responsible for such conduct, but we will say something more about that as we move on. In paragraph 58 of the indictment and paragraph 313 of the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution states that General Lazarevic as the commander of the Pristina Corps had a de jure and de facto control over VJ brigades and smaller VJ units that were part of the Pristina Corps and other units from other corps that were attached to the Pristina Corps. Such allegations on the part of the Prosecution are absolutely incorrect, and this conclusion is based on the evidence called by the Prosecution. Prosecution Witness Aleksandar Vasiljevic in his testimony on the 23rd of January, 2007, claims quite resolutely that some brigades and units were not subordinated to the Pristina Corps. That's at page 8963, line 5. Furthermore, the decision to engage units from other corps was made by the superior command, and it was completely legitimate and in accordance with the law. The Defence would like to add here that General Lazarevic had the de jure control only over those units that were part of the Pristina Corps. As regards the de facto control, we have to say that the commanders of the subordinate brigades in the Pristina Corps were the ones who had the de facto control over their subordinate units, battalions, platoons, and companies on the ground. The Prosecution also alleges that after the imminent threat of war was declared on the 23rd of March, 1999, General Lazarevic gained control over the military territorial units that carried out military operations, the MUP units that were involved in the military operations, and armed non-Albanian population in Kosovo that took care of local security. In order to show that there is no evidence to support such Prosecution allegations, we will give you some examples. The Defence wishes to believe that this position of the Prosecution is a consequence of the erroneous linguistic interpretation of Article 17 of the Law on Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Exhibit Number is P985. In this article it is stipulated quite clearly that in the case of an imminent threat of war, state of war, or state of emergency, the units and organs of the Ministry of Interior may - I stress "may" - be used to carry out combat tasks or to engage in combat or to offer armed resistance. The word "may" indicates that this is just an option, and it does not stem from this wording that they must be subordinated. This argument and this interpretation of this law is confirmed by Prosecution evidence. Prosecution Witness Aleksandar Vasiljevic in his testimony before the Tribunal claims that there never was the resubordination of MUP or its units to the Yugoslav Army. The information, the order, the report to that effect was sent by the commander of the 3rd Army to the Chief of General Staff, and that's Exhibit P1459. Prosecution Witness Dusan Loncar in his testimony states quite unequivocally that MUP never commanded the army and that the army never commanded the MUP. So he also confirms that there never was any resubordination, that's at page 7609, line 25; page 7611, lines 1 to 9. If one could say that all those witnesses that we quoted were members of the VJ, we could offer in support of our arguments that Witness Ljubinko Cvetic, chief in MUP, who confirmed that MUP had never been resubordinated to the Yugoslav Army. That's at page 8140, lines 21 to 25. With reference to military territorial units and the civilian protection and defence, unambiguous evidence has been presented from the standpoint of the subordination of these units to the Pristina Corps. Prosecution Witness Zlatomir Pesic said that the use of military territorial detachments which were part of the military districts was optional and that their use depended on the decision of the brigade commander. That's page 7237, lines 16 to 19. This witness goes on to say that units of the civilian protection and civilian defence, with reference to organisation, had a place within the Ministry of Defence, and as such they had no connection with the VJ. That's page 7184, lines 24 to 25; page 7185, lines 1 to 3. This witness says that such detachments even had their own separate chain of command which ran through the sector leaders of the Ministry of Defence from Kosovo, or rather, leader Ilic up to the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade without any points of contact with the Pristina Corps. That's page 7184, lines 24 to 25; page 7185, line 1 to 3. Furthermore, Witness Aleksandar Vasiljevic, whom we have referred to more than once, in his testimony before this Tribunal on the 23rd of January, 2007, also confirmed that units of the civilian protection and civilian defence were not subordinated to the Pristina Corps but were rather under the command of the Ministry of Defence. That's page 8963, lines 1 to 5. It is quite clear then that the above-mentioned claim by the Prosecution has no basis in the evidence that has been adduced and that the Prosecution has failed to prove which units under the command of the Pristina Corps committed possible crimes. The Prosecution also submits in its pre-trial brief that there were joint operations of the VJ and the MUP and that the plans and orders issued by the corps commanders referred to such joint operations. Our Defence does not deny that there were certain operations on the ground where there was cooperation and coordination between the MUP and the VJ. But there was no resubordination within the scope of these operations. Both the MUP and the VJ retained their own lines of command -- their own chains of command and their own chains of planning. This is also shown by the evidence we have already referred to; however, we can also find confirmation for this in an analysis of the orders issued by the commander of the -- and commanders of the Pristina Corps where joint operations are envisaged. However, it is quite clear that specific tasks for such operations were always aimed against the KLA and that they were issued exclusively to military units. And it is only from the military units of the corps that feedback, or rather, reports and briefings on the action carried out are required. One of the elements of command is reporting on the implementation of the order through a combat report. It is clear that only corps units were asked to submit such reports. Not a single combat report goes beyond the scope of the tasks that the Pristina Corps had. Let us remember that General Vasiljevic evaluated these documents as highly professional and very precisely drawn up. It is correct that certain orders envisage coordination and joint action, but let us reiterate this only pertains to actions aimed against the armed KLA. And according to the testimony of Witness Bislim Zyrapi, in the time-period these orders referred to, the KLA had grown to 18.000 soldiers, page 5959, lines 12 to 19. Is coordination and cooperation between the legitimate organs of a state irregular and illegal, especially when it is carried out in order to implement a constitutional provision on the protection of the territorial integrity and sovereignty of an internationally recognised state? The answer to this is clear, even without adducing special evidence to prove it. Of course such coordination and cooperation are not unlawful. They are necessary in a situation when forces being used in an attempt to cut off and separate off part of an internationally recognised territory which has its internationally recognised borders, and these are assertions that the Prosecution has also confirmed through the evidence it has adduced. The Defence would like to remind the Chamber that Witness Maisonneuve, when asked to comment on what we have just been referring to, pointed out that coordination between the VJ and the MUP was certainly necessary and he evaluated it as professional. He went on to point out that every operation implying the participation of the VJ and the MUP must entail close cooperation so that each formation knows about the plans of the other in order to avoid so-called friendly fire. Witness Maisonneuve also stressed the need to carry out coordination in advance of such operations in order to establish a clear description of the responsibilities of each formation. That's page 11183, lines 13 to 23. Prosecution Witness Colonel Crosland confirmed that based on his experience which he gained serving throughout the world, it is to be expected that there would be coordination and cooperation between various elements of the MUP and VJ forces in Kosovo in order to avoid friendly fire. Page 9815, lines 8 to 19. And finally, Witness Dusan Loncar pointed out in no uncertain terms the importance of coordination, cooperation, and exchange of information between the MUP and the VJ and even the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He said that such cooperation was not only necessary but indispensable. He went on to say, especially in view of the activities of the KLA, that full cooperation of these two armed components of the state was needed in the carrying out of combat operations. That's page 7612, lines 15 to 25; and 7613, lines 1 to 5. The Prosecution in its pre-trial brief further alleges that the plans and orders issued by the Pristina Corps in connection with operations within the relevant time-period included continuous use of troops and commanders which the accused Lazarevic knew to have been involved in crimes committed in the course of 1998, and that rather change tactics as soon as he took over command of the Pristina Corps in 1999, General Lazarevic ordered the engagement of these same troops in the same way that led to crimes in 1998. Such sweeping, across-the-board statements by the Prosecution in its pre-trial brief are absolutely unfounded in view of the evidence adduced before this Tribunal and the facts that we consider to have been established. The Defence would first like to point out that the Prosecution has not in any serious way in a manner envisaged by criminal law even tried to establish which crimes were actually committed in the course of 1998 or who was responsible for them. The Prosecution attempted to tender newspaper articles, books, or brochures which were rejected because of their lack of weight or probative value. When we look back on the evidence and the testimonies of the witnesses heard, it is clear to any reasonable trier of fact that the Prosecution has failed by far to prove this. We have provided numerous examples of testimony by high-ranking military and political officials who all unanimously confirmed that in 1998 the behaviour of the VJ was professional and correct. The Defence further submits that General Lazarevic was not the one who ordered the use of VJ and its units. Such orders on the use of units, pursuant to the rules of the use of forces, have to come from a high superior command. Witness Vasiljevic in his testimony on pages 8915, lines 20 to 25, and 8916, lines 1 to 5, on the 23rd of January, 2007, confirmed that the decision on the use of the army has to be made at the highest command post and certainly not at corps level. This might be a good place to mention the generally known fact which is common knowledge and need not even be proved that a subordinate commander is duty-bound to carry out orders coming from the superior command in every case except when such an order requires the subordinate commander to commit a crime. Needless to say, the Prosecution has not even tried to specify which order, either issued by the superior command or by General Lazarevic as the corps commander, ordered a subordinate command to carry out a crime. The Prosecution was unable to prove this because, simply, there is no such order. The assessment that those orders, which their own key witnesses assessed as professional and very correct, contain ulterior motivates and hidden intentions to carry out crimes are pure speculation and this cannot rise to the level of a proved fact before this Tribunal. It is clear that the conclusion presented by the Prosecution in its pre-trial brief, that this use of troops is evidence that Lazarevic instigated the perpetration of future crimes and therefore contributed to the perpetration of crimes through which the criminal purpose was achieved absolutely fails to hold water. Furthermore, the Prosecution suggests that General Lazarevic, as Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, was informed by international observers in 1998 of crimes committed by forces under his command. This claim is absolutely incorrect. It is not necessary to go into all the assessments by high-ranking international officials of the behaviour of the VJ, both towards the missions that were present in Kosovo and with reference to the behaviour of troops on the ground. What we feel should be mentioned here is that General Lazarevic, as Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, attended a meeting in early December, more precisely the 4th of December, 1998, between General Drewienkiewicz and the military representative General Loncar, at which the topic on the agenda was how to inspect VJ and MUP forces by the OSCE, and no crimes were mentioned. Apart from this meeting, at which General Lazarevic did not participate in the discussion, as testified to by Drewienkiewicz, General Lazarevic attended no other meetings with OSCE officials or officials of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Neither of the witnesses we have mentioned spoke of any other meeting attended by General Lazarevic, none of the witnesses confirmed that Lazarevic attended any other meeting, and Witness Shaun Byrnes, when asked directly whether he was ever in contact with General Lazarevic, said that he had never contacted Lazarevic and that nobody even mentioned him. That's page 12201, lines 8 to 14. The testimony of this witness shows how numerous the meetings were which he attended from -- all the way up to March 1999 and the beginning of NATO air-strikes. General Lazarevic is charged in the indictment with failing to take any steps to prevent crimes and that he also accepted volunteers into his troops. The Defence wishes to draw the Chamber's attention to Exhibit P1479, which is an order issued by the Supreme Command Staff dated the 7th of April, 1999, and it has already been referred to by my colleague Mr. Sepenuk, where the Supreme Command Staff stresses the importance of volunteers going through triage, through training centres, and through all kinds of screening. And I will not reiterate what Mr. Sepenuk has already said, although I had intended to speak about this. I will therefore move on now and speak of the testimony of Witness Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who also stated that there were two reception centres for volunteers, in Belgrade and you can see this in Exhibit P1479 which has already been referred to. These were in Grocka near Belgrade and this was organised by the 1st Army; and the second location for the reception of volunteers was Medja near Nis, this was organised by the command of the Nis Military District. Prosecution Witness Aleksandar Vasiljevic spoke about this issue and confirmed the existence of these two reception centres where volunteers were screened because of the bad experience from the preceding period. 50 per cent of the volunteers who applied were rejected right away. They did not pass through the check and were not received into the VJ. Also in evidence is Prosecution Exhibit P1938, that's a report by the command of the 3rd Army about the reception and the assignment of volunteers in the 3rd Army. This document shows quite clearly that there were such two reception centres. So these exhibits show quite clearly that the Prosecution's allegation that General Lazarevic was the one who admitted volunteers into the Pristina Corps army does not hold water. The reception of volunteers and their assignment was conducted in accordance with the law at higher levels. Did General Lazarevic do anything about the volunteers? Well, you've heard about that from Mr. Sepenuk, my colleague, and I would just like to remind you of Exhibit P1938, a document originating from the 3rd Army command, and Exhibit P1943, a document originating from the Supreme Command Staff, where we read the following: "A few days after the reception, 25 volunteers were turned back from the PRK and seven were detained because of rebellion, murder, rape, refusal to comply with the orders, and desertion." General Lazarevic took immediate measures when any irregularities regarding the reception of the volunteers were observed and he took measures to arrest those volunteers who committed criminal offences, and he also take measures -- took measures whenever he had any knowledge from his subordinate brigade commanders that VJ officers and rank-and-file soldiers should be prosecuted if there was any suspicion that they had committed any criminal act. There is documentary evidence and also testimony by witnesses to support this claim. We have document 5D84 that's been admitted into evidence, it's a combat report issued by the PRK command and sent to the 3rd Army command, where in paragraphs 5 it states: "In the previous days -- in the previous day, 32 criminal reports were filed against perpetrators of criminal offences: Eight murders; one abuse; three attempted murders; theft of vehicle; theft, six instances; and absence without leave, 12 instances." Again, in Prosecution Exhibit P2617, that's again a combat report submitted to the 3rd Army command by the PRK command in paragraph 5 it states -- it is stated: "In the previous day, six criminal reports were filed against perpetrators of criminal offences." Furthermore, Prosecution Exhibit 5962 [as interpreted], it's an overview of criminal proceedings launched against persons responsible for criminal offences within the area of responsibility of just one brigade, that's the 549th Motorised Brigade, it is stated that 132 criminal reports were filed, almost half of them were -- concern serious or severe criminal offences. Yet, the Prosecution claims that in most instances the criminal offences were failure to respond to the call-up. This overview for the 549th Motorised Brigade shows that criminal reports were filed under numbers 103, 104, 105, and 106. You can see that four members of the Yugoslav Army were prosecuted and convicted of war crimes. So measures were not taken only against persons who failed to respond to the call-up. This overview from the 549th Motorised Brigade confirms this, confirms that serious efforts were taken to prosecute rank-and-file soldiers and officers alike and this very same overview shows that when it comes to the four members there were two soldiers, one captain, and one major. They were prosecuted and convicted. And the major who is the ranking soldier in this case was sentenced to 14 years, the captain was sentenced to nine years, and the two soldiers were sentenced, two privates were sentenced to five and two years respectively. Exhibit 5 -- Exhibit P1268, an order issued by the commander of the Pristina Corps dated the 30th of April, 1999, orders that after anti-terrorist combat actions are over, that clean-up of the theatre should be carried out and this -- that this task is given to a unit that was also tasked with carrying out anti-terrorist combat actions. In paragraph 2 of this order it is stated that after combat is over, investigative actions are to be taken if there are grounds for suspicion or if there are any indicia that the criminal offence had been committed or to clarify any relevant facts if it is possible -- if it is necessary for the judicial investigative organs to directly observe the -- what is going on. Finally, in paragraph 3, it is stated that the unit responsible for the carrying out of anti-terrorist actions also has within its remit the conduct of investigative activities. Military judicial organs take investigative actions only in cases when a VJ unit carried out the anti-terrorist operations or when there was reason for -- to suspect that the criminal offence was committed by a member of the VJ. We have to say something about Exhibit P1182, this is a report filed by the PRK command, dated the 15th of May, 1999, about the crime trends among professional active-duty servicemen. This was sent to the subordinate units, and this report clearly shows that in the period between the 24th of March, 1999, and the 10th of May, 1999, proceedings were launched before wartime military courts against 91 active-duty servicemen. This document is not a mere report, and this can be seen from the last paragraph where it says that: "The commission of such and similar criminal offences on the part of the officers and non-commissioned officers in the state of war is deviant conduct that threatens to seriously undermine the morale and combat-readiness in the VJ units and nothing needs to be said about the influence it may have on the subordinates." It goes on to say that the perpetration of such and similar criminal offences, particularly on the part of officers, to a large extent besmirches the reputation of the VJ and the trust of the people in the army. When we talk about clean-up operations and investigations, Prosecution witness said something about this topic, Dr. Gordana Tomasevic, at page 7804, lines 18 to 25, when she was asked about the exhumations she carried out at the Bijelo Polje site and later on at the Malo Ribare site on the order of the investigative military judges she said that both exhumations had been carried out in the presence of a military investigative judge and that everything had been done in accordance with the law on criminal procedure. Finally, Prosecution witness General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, whom we've quoted so many times, gave a very extensive and clear statement about these issues. In his testimony he explained that there was a triple line of reporting on potential crimes. One required that the commander of the PRK should submit reports to the commander of the 3rd Army; the second line was -- linked the security organs of the corps and the security organ in the 3rd Army; and the third one linked military judicial organs. That's at page 8964, lines 6 to 13. This witness stated quite certain -- in no uncertain terms that all the reports of the security organs on the crimes that were prosecuted by the judicial organs, with the exception of the Gornja Klina incident because it was impossible to do so because the Albanians took control over this area. But, according to what this witness knows, this case was finally brought to trial before the military court in Nis that's at page 8789, line 25, and page 8790, lines 1 to 15. The same witness goes on to say that there was no intent on the part of the VJ to conceal the crimes, and he also stresses that after General Farkas visited the security organs of the Pristina Corps, gave high marks to those organs, stressing that all the personnel in those formations should be given a promotion. That's at page 8976, lines 21 to 25; page 8977, lines 19 to 25. The Defence would like to submit or to note that in answer to an explicit question, General Vasiljevic -- when General Vasiljevic was asked whether General Lazarevic notified the higher command after he learned about the crimes and submitted criminal reports to the judicial organs and whether he could have done anything else, Witness Vasiljevic said he met his obligations by doing that; there was nothing else he could do. That's at page 8969, lines 18 to 23. The Defence has to ask itself whether any reasonable trier of fact could conclude that the Prosecution did prove beyond reasonable doubt that General Vladimir Lazarevic participated in the JCE, in the planning, instigation, and ordering of the concealment of crimes on the part of the PRK or, indeed, instigated and gave legitimacy of the crimes against Kosovo Albanians by failing to report or investigate those crimes. We will quite clearly state here that we firmly believe that the Prosecution has failed to do so and that the trier of fact cannot find this. Finally, the Prosecution alleges that General Lazarevic alternatively aided and abetted the commission of such crimes because he allowed and facilitated the participation of VJ personnel and materiel in combat actions in Kosovo. This contention by the Prosecution is both illogical and contradictory. The Prosecution itself claims that Lazarevic allowed the participation of the VJ in combat actions. In addition to the evidence we referred to above on the use of forces and the compliance with the orders, it is unclear why it is illegal and irregular to use a military in combat. The Prosecution goes on to suggest that he failed to take any disciplinary measures against VJ or MUP personnel who had committed crimes in Kosovo, and that by doing that he encouraged and gave moral support to the direct perpetrators of crimes against Kosovo Albanians. The Defence has already analysed the evidence that points quite clearly to the fact that General Lazarevic had no powers over MUP personnel and was not able and/or authorised to punish them. There is ample evidence referred to above to show that the military judicial organs had no powers to punish MUP personnel. An analysis of the reports on the criminal offences that were prosecuted and the criminal reports that were filed clearly and unequivocally indicate that military judicial organs had no power to prosecute MUP personnel. The Defence has already said something about measures taken against VJ personnel in the Pristina Corps, and we claim therefore that the Prosecution has not furnished any evidence for the alternative charges against General Lazarevic on the basis of aiding and abetting. The Prosecution claims that there was a joint criminal enterprise; that General Lazarevic was aware, that he knew, of that plan; and that he did possess the intent to commit the crimes he's charged with in the indictment. The Defence would like, once again, to stress that it is our firm position that no plan targeting the civilian Albanian population existed and that the Prosecution failed to prove that such a plan existed. If a plan existed aimed against the civilian Albanian population, then we believe firmly that General Lazarevic was not aware of this plan, that he didn't know about that plan, and that he did not demonstrate an intent to participate in such a plan. Although we are convinced that Prosecution Witness Ratomir Tanic's evidence will not be given any major weight, General Lazarevic must refer to parts of his testimony out of an abundance of caution, as my learned colleague Mr. Sepenuk noted in his address. At page 6756 of the transcript, the witness confirmed that Lazarevic did not have a full picture of the events because he was not a member of the State Commission. There is an abundance of evidence indicating the large number, the tactics of the conduct of combat, and other characteristics of the activities of the armed KLA which, quite justifiably, could twist, warp the picture on the existence of some kind of goal which was not the fight to preserve the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the FRY. We will go back and refer to the testimony of Bislim Zyrapi, who said that at the relevant time-period the KLA had grown to as many as 18.000 fighters. The same witness, as we have already said, said that the KLA retreated together with the population. He goes on to say that from the beginning of NATO air-strikes, Serb forces attacked KLA positions. All these statements were made on pages 5989, line 25; and page 5990, lines 1 to 5. Furthermore, this witness said that among the KLA fighters there were also women and that from the beginning of the NATO air-strikes, the KLA had the assistance of the Government of Albania, page 6180, line 1 to 13. When asked where KLA fighters were located, this same witness said that for the most part they were accommodated in schools, collective facilities, and houses depending on the situation in the region, page 6181, lines 24 to 25; page 6182, lines 1 to 3. The same witness goes on to say that local staffs which were made up of the local population were supplied and armed by the KLA. He also points out that they - these local staffs - wore civilian uniforms because they did not have any military uniforms page 6232, lines 20 to 23. Witness General Maisonneuve, in his testimony before this Tribunal, spoke of a strong KLA presence in Kosovo, page 11111, lines 8 to 12; and further he testified it would be correct to conclude that the KLA used villages as its basis, 11135, lines 3 to 9. Witness Colonel Richard Ciaglinski, a member of the KVM mission on page 6902, lines 16 to 25, confirmed that during the sojourn of the mission in Kosovo the KLA carried out ethnic cleansing of Serb villages and that during the negotiations in Paris the KLA intensified its attacks. General Klaus Naumann, another witness, additionally confirmed that it was exceptionally difficult to protect the civilian population because the rebels were also wearing civilian clothes and were mixed with the civilian population, page 8319, lines 22 to 25. Colonel Crosland, in his testimony, confirmed that on the ground the KLA implemented a strategy described in Mao Zedong's book and that it first established its bases in villages and then expected the NATO intervention. Page 9899 [Realtime transcript read in error "9895"], line 25; page 9900 [Realtime transcript read in error "9890"], lines 1 to 9. Your Honours, I have perhaps some 15 minutes and I think this may be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you so much. In order to confirm what you have said just now, I will have to ask for two corrections to be made in the transcript. May I make the following corrections. Page 28 of the transcript, line 17, the exhibit that we quoted was P962 rather than 5962. So it is P rather than 5. And towards the very end, or rather, just before the break on page 35, line 22, it should read page 9899, line 25, and page 9900, lines 1 through 9. Once again, I apologise to the interpreters for having caused them this trouble by reading so fast and I will do my best, of course, not to have this happen again. Your Honours, we stopped at a certain part of the transcript which has to do with the nature of -- of the struggle waged by the KLA against the Serb forces, and we would like to say that General Dusan Loncar, a Prosecution witness, otherwise a representative of the federal government for cooperation with the OSCE mission, on page 7617, lines 17 through 23, confirms that the KLA took advantage of the presence of the Kosovo Verification Mission to, as he put it, re-organise, consolidate, arm, and prepare for struggle against the Serb forces. The same witness further on, confirms that the KLA often used civilians as a human shield, primarily women and children. The page reference is 7617, lines 24 and 25, then page 7618, lines 1 through 9. This witness also adds that at the time when he was in contact with the Kosovo Verification Mission, especially with General Drewienkiewicz, frequent references were made to the forthcoming spring offensive of the KLA, although in the pre-trial brief reference is made to the forthcoming spring offensive of the Serb forces. The reference for this is on transcript page 7618, lines 14 through 21. As for what Witness Loncar said on the arming of the KLA and preparing for a fight against the Serb forces, that is confirmed by Witness Shaun Byrnes as well on page 12217, lines 24 and 25 and page 12218, lines 1 and 2. This witness says that it was well known among all the international observers in Kosovo that the Albanians were arming prior to, during, and after the October agreement. The testimony of the mentioned witnesses, notably General Loncar, is corroborated by Prosecution Exhibit P641, admitted on the 4th of December, 2006, which constitutes a report of the liaison officer of the KVM marked DZ8, where when events are described in the zone of Nerodimlje, it is stated that there was a conflict between the KLA and the security forces and that a military operation took place in order to remove the KLA from the region. Further on, it is stated in the report that during the preparations for this operation the brigade commander of the KLA from that area made it impossible for the UNHCR to evacuate displaced persons, which was interpreted as a cynical attempt to use Albanian civilians as a human shield. All of the above mentioned clearly and unequivocally shows that the Defence thesis is right; namely, that even if there was some kind of a plan - and we repeat and we claim that there was no such thing and that was not proven either - all this evidence clearly indicates that in such a situation, even if there were a kind of plan, it would have been virtually impossible or very difficult in this situation and bearing in mind the position that my client held it would be very difficult to recognise that kind of a plan, that is to say, bearing in mind KLA tactics, the use of civilians, instant attacks. The plan, as the Prosecution says in the indictment and its pre-trial brief from the point of view of the position of the commander of the Pristina Corps faced with all these facts, it is very hard to discern any such thing and we need to have firm evidence that there was such a plan, or rather, that General Lazarevic knew of the existence of such a plan and had an intention of taking part in such a plan. In order to support what we've been saying now in terms of intent, we are going to invoke P2004, which constitutes a combat report of the command of the Pristina Corps to the command of the 3rd Army, dated the 13th of April, 1999; namely, that some -- this is 20 days after the NATO bombing started. And then in paragraph 4, which refers to the morale of the members of the corps, the following is stated: "The morale of the corps personnel is very good and stable. The increasingly pronounced stands of world political factors that the question of Kosovo and Metohija can and must be resolved by political means has had a positive effect on the morale of the troops." Is that not sufficient evidence in terms of General Lazarevic's intent? Encouraging the army and reporting to his superiors that such solutions, political solutions, are generally accepted within the corps. Witness Dusan Loncar, in response to a direct question as to whether he knew that there ever was any plan to attack the civilian population and to expel it from Kosovo and Metohija, gives the following answer: "First and foremost, knowing the people who were at the head of this corps, Generals Lazarevic and Pavkovic, as well as the commanders and persons who headed the organs, I would rule out any possibility in that sense, and I think that would have been highly inappropriate." The page reference is 7687, lines 9 through 15. The Defence cannot but add at this point as well that it was precisely it was this witness who said in response to a direct question to the effect whether while he was in Kosovo he had occasion to assess the professional conduct of General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic; and if so, what his assessment was, he answered that he knew General Pavkovic from their student days, from the military academy, and that he can say quite freely that he is an exceptionally professional military leader and an exceptional general. As for General Lazarevic, Witness Loncar says that he can state what the majority of the officers of the Army of Yugoslavia believe, that he is a general par excellence. Your Honours, I do apologise to you, a typo was made in the references for this, so I don't have the exact page reference in my text. So may I give you the exact page reference later for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the honourable Trial Chamber finds probative value in -- for the testimony of Witness -- Prosecution Witness K73, when assessing the intent of General Lazarevic, you have to look at his testimony. What happened was very unusual. He asked whether he could address the accused General Lazarevic directly, and then this witness said that for General Lazarevic all -- as far as General Lazarevic was concerned, all officers had a very high regard for him, they consider him to be a professional soldier, a good, honest, honourable man, and a strong commander. In the personal view of this witness, General Lazarevic was never a politician or simply career-oriented. He was a soldier, a military leader, who defended his country. Furthermore, this witness gave his own assessment that General Lazarevic does not belong in this courtroom and that it was an honour for him to have served his country under General Lazarevic's command. The transcript page is 3415. In this stage of the proceedings, highest standards are sought, but we claim that the Prosecution did not present evidence and prove the intent of General Lazarevic to take part in a possible joint criminal enterprise and we repeat yet again that this never existed. Again, very briefly, the Defence of General Lazarevic wishes to say a few words about responsibility in respect of Article 7(3). Of course we have already referred to some evidence in this context, so we are not going to repeat it yet again. The Defence claims that the Prosecution did not manage to prove that General Lazarevic omitted to exercise his own authority and duties to prevent his subordinates from committing a crime, or rather, that he omitted to punish them afterwards. There is ample evidence that we pointed out during our previous remarks when we spoke about responsibility in respect of Article 1, especially in terms of aiding and abetting, and they are applicable in terms of assessing responsibility in relation to Article 7(3). We believe that by analysing this evidence we showed, or rather, by referring to the relevant sections, we showed that the Prosecution did not prove that General Lazarevic omitted to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the perpetration of crimes and punish the perpetrators. There was evidence concerning the return of volunteers and the filing of criminal reports against officers and reporting to subordinate units to refrain from the commission of crimes and to apply provisions of international humanitarian law. And at any rate, these are indispensable and reasonable measures to prevent crimes, or rather, to punish perpetrators; and this punishment was within the authority of military judicial organs. Again, I would like to refer to the testimony of General Vasiljevic, a -- a witness here, namely that General Lazarevic took everything within his powers in terms of prosecution and bringing criminal charges against perpetrators. The Defence, once again, would like to remind this Trial Chamber that although General Lazarevic was physically and in terms of the line -- chain of command removed from the centre where the -- the top leadership of the state was, also as the commander of the Pristina Corps he was removed from immediate action in terms of his units in the field itself. We wish to remind you that in terms of chain of command, under General Lazarevic as commander of the Pristina Corps there were commanders of brigades; and under them battalion commanders; then commanders of platoons and companies. All of this clearly indicates that taking measures directly depended on the degree and quantity of information that came from subordinate units. If we bear in mind - and I will now say something that hasn't really been verified - Kosovo is in territory larger than the Netherlands in view of the Defence. And if we look at the strength of the forces on the ground, the question is whether General Lazarevic could, indeed, have known of every irregularity or every crime that was actually committed on the ground. It is quite obvious, again on the basis of evidence we quoted above, that General Lazarevic responded to every incident, illegal incident, that he had been notified of, and the Prosecution failed to establish and prove that General Lazarevic failed to take measures to prevent a crime or to punish perpetrators in any of the cases that he was aware of. On the basis of everything we presented above, the Defence of General Lazarevic claims that the Prosecution has failed to prove that our client is responsible under Article 7(1) and under Article 7(3) for crimes alleged in the indictment in Counts 1 through 5, and that is why we move that the honourable Trial Chamber acquit General Vladimir Lazarevic of all five counts of the indictment and to set him free. Thank you very much, Your Honours.
