utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court, as you know, I am Dan Ivetic, and I will be presenting the Rule 98 bis submissions on behalf of the Defence team of Sreten Lukic, the sixth named accused in these proceedings. A great deal of the general legal arguments and comments about the deficiencies of the Prosecution's case have already been set forth concisely by my colleagues, so I'll try not to unduly repeat those submissions, save where I believe it is helpful to highlight regarding the various submissions that I will be setting forth. One thing that immediately is evident from a review of the indictment and the record of evidence that has been led by the Prosecution in this case is that the picture of events is not the same as was envisaged in the third amended indictment, nor even in the opening statements of my colleague Mr. Hannis, with which we commenced these proceedings. Indeed, I would respectfully submit that among the things that has been proven by the presentment of evidence to date has been how inaccurate and flawed witness statements and supporting material forming the indictment can be. Just as we could not take for granted the material set forth in the witness statements without scrutiny in cross-examination, likewise, we submit, that it is necessary to scrutinise the indictment in light of the evidence that has been led as the picture that has emerged does not, in fact, support the allegations of the indictment against our client, and therefore acquittal is proper and necessary under Rule 98 bis to avoid injustice. The importance of giving a thorough application of Rule 98 bis to this case cannot be stressed enough. A cornerstone principle of the Tribunal is that the Prosecution bears the burden throughout the case of proving the guilt of an accused beyond a reasonable doubt. If the Prosecution fails to clear the first hurdle of establishing a case that requires an answer from the accused in his Defence case, the burden clearly has not been discharged and the case against him must be dismissed. Likewise, if the goal of these proceedings has been the ascertainment of the truth, the evidence adduced by the Prosecution must be assessed as to the truth it has revealed and if it is wholly inconsistent with the allegations of guilt made by the Prosecution in the indictment, the charges against Mr. Lukic must be stricken at this stage. I think it's important to highlight one of the earlier 98 bis decisions in the Prosecutor versus Kordic and Cerkez of 6th April 2000 at paragraph 28 where the Trial Chamber held that the Rule 98 bis motion ought to be granted where the Prosecution's case has: "Completely broken down, either on its own presentation or as a result of such fundamental questions being raised through cross-examination as to the reliability and credibility of witnesses that the Prosecution is left without a case." Respectfully, the instant circumstances are precisely those with respect to the allegations against Mr. Lukic. As my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan cited to the law from the most recent 98 bis cases, if -- the Prosecution's case cannot survive at this stage if it is based upon evidence incapable of belief. Now, by way of introduction and overview, it is respectfully submitted that the case presented by the Prosecution has failed to establish the fundamentally required elements of the crimes charged against Sreten Lukic. The Prosecution, respectfully, submitted no evidence that Sreten Lukic in concert with other individuals identified in the indictment planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in the commission of crimes charged in the indictment at either the preparatory or execution phases, whereby his participation in formulating a criminal plan and endorsing a plan proposed by others was substantial, as required by the relevant standards for a joint criminal enterprise from the jurisprudence of both this Tribunal and the ICTR. We submit that while a reasonable trier of fact could potentially find under the evidence presented that one or more of the alleged crimes in question were committed by someone, it could not find beyond a reasonable doubt that Sreten Lukic was involved in or intended the results of these crimes. I will go through the charged incidents from the indictment to demonstrate this fact more clearly later in our submissions. The Prosecution presented no evidence that Sreten Lukic by his acts and conduct prompted other individuals identified in the indictment or specified through the evidence to commit the crimes charged in Counts 1 through 5 of the indictment. Likewise, the Prosecution presented no evidence that Lukic's acts or conduct constituted a contributing factor to the conduct of the physical and actual perpetrators of the crimes alleged. There is no evidence before this Chamber that Mr. Lukic intended to provoke and induce the commission of these crimes or that he was aware of the substantial likelihood that the commission of these crimes would be a probable consequence of any acts and conduct on his part. Simply put, the evidence fails to uphold any possible liability for instigating crimes either. The Prosecution has not adduced proper evidence that Sreten Lukic issued any criminal orders to individuals who are alleged to have been the perpetrators of crimes set forth in the indictment; indeed to the contrary, the relevant evidence presented shows that Lukic never knowingly or wilfully issued any orders to commit crimes nor, indeed, did he have authority over persons alleged to have committed crimes. The Prosecution case has failed to establish with requisite evidence that Mr. Lukic aided or abetted any individuals alleged to have perpetrated crimes. As is clear, Mr. Lukic never rendered any assistance and, rather, per the testimony of K84, one of the insider MUP star witnesses for the Prosecution, among others, Mr. Lukic was instrumental in the commencement of inquiries into alleged misconduct and an establishment of an Ministry of Internal Affairs Working Group to investigate MUP personnel relative to the clandestine transport of bodies to Batajnica and elsewhere in Serbia. We can find this from transcript page 5214, line 21 through transcript page 5215, line 6. The evidence of this Prosecution witness, K84, established that Sreten Lukic told this Working Group to investigate everyone, including himself, to determine the truth and that he positively cooperated in the investigation. This is from the transcript page 5216, lines 5 through 17. This evidence flies in the face of the general allegations in the indictment and does not correspond with someone who had any fears or guilt on his mind. The requisite mens rea or intent of Mr. Lukic to commit or conceal crimes has not been established by the evidence. The Prosecution simply did not adduce evidence that demonstrated that during the relevant time-period of the indictment, that is March to June 1999, that Sreten Lukic knew of persons intending to commit crimes or that he was aware or intended that any of his acts assisted the principal offenders in these crimes. Now, I'd like to start our highlighting of various matters of evidence with respect to Article 7(3) liability which is alleged against Mr. Lukic to be -- to establish such a form of liability, the three-pronged test must be satisfied which was enumerated by my colleague Mr. Ackerman yesterday. All three prongs of the test are important for scrutinising the evidence against Mr. Lukic and, respectfully, the Prosecution has failed to demonstrate any of the three prongs to the requisite degree necessary to uphold a conviction and to survive the 98 bis stage. Conspicuously, I must point out, the Prosecution failed to call a single expert witness to delineate and opine upon the structure, functioning, and lines of command of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia under the laws and regulations and legislation in place during the relevant time-period. According to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, much of the allegations about the functioning of the Ministry of Internal Affairs was to be proven via a purported expert witness. Not only did no such expert materialise, but the Prosecution instead tried to obtain unqualified testimony from persons with no training in internal affairs and no formal knowledge of the laws pertaining to the Ministry of the Interior, essentially, to give layperson opinions and conjecture about the functioning of the MUP, speculation really. Multiple KVM, KDOM personnel, as well as purported VJ insiders were questioned about the functioning of the MUP. This is interesting insofar as all these witnesses came from military backgrounds and presented military terminology and military understanding to express their beliefs and understanding about how the MUP functioned. Even more interesting, although having the opportunity to examine several MUP officers and officials that testified, such as K84 and Caslav Golubovic, for instance, about the functioning of the MUP, the Prosecution failed to take advantage of that opportunity and relied upon a vision basically painting the MUP as if it were just another type of army formation with army ranks and positions and an army or military stove-top chain of command to the top. Such a flawed approach is apparent from the very indictment. At paragraph 7 of the indictment states that Lukic was appointed as "head of the MUP staff." Now, throughout the trial terms such as "chief" or "commander" have been used to describe Lukic. However, the sole bit of evidence relied upon by the Prosecution regarding this allegation, P1505, sets forth plainly that the true position of Sreten Lukic is in the original Serbian language "rukovodilac", which in English can mean manager or administrator or head. It does not mean the same thing as "nacelnik", the Serbian word for chief which describes the function or position of the heads of the secretariats for internal affairs in Serbia and Kosovo and this distinction is vital within the police structure as it makes a difference to the authority and power and body within that position. Simple logic dictates that insofar as "rukovodjenje", the verb form of rukovodilac or management is one of the powers of nacelnik or chief but that a nacelnik also has command ability which is distinct from rukovodjenje implies that a rukovodilac, one who undertakes rukovodjenje, has a much narrower scope of superior authority. This is confirmed by the evidence led by the Prosecution, specifically P1737, the Law on Internal Affairs, which sets forth the powers embodied within a nacelnik. Now, the problem presented by this error in thinking and error in using terminology and the deficiency of using military-minded persons to describe the functioning of the MUP can be seen from other laws that have been introduced into evidence by the Prosecution. Unlike the Ministry of Interior, the army - in this case the VJ - according to Exhibit P984, is defined as having command based on the principles of unity of command, unity of superiors, and obligations to execute the decisions and orders of superior officers. The allegations made by the Prosecution against the MUP follow this same model, but on the other hand the law specifies a different model, specifically P1823, the law on state administration, specifies that ministries are state administrative organs and that the minister represents the ministry, the minister organises and provides for the efficient and legal work of the ministry and the minister decides about the rights, duties, and responsibilities of the employees of the ministry, with the minister ultimately responsible for his function and the work of the ministry. Thus, rather than having a strict unity of command as understood in the military sense, rather than having unity of superiors, a ministry employee can have whatever duties and authorities are given to him by the minister. Importantly, the Chamber will recall throughout the trial that various MUP witnesses testified that persons with lower ranks such as captain or major actually were superior in power and authority to persons with higher ranks, such as colonel or general, based upon the authority conferred to them by their specific appointment. I would recall witnesses K84 and Caslav Golubovic, for example, on this point. Now, such fundamental features of the relevant laws introduced by the Prosecution were either ignored, misunderstood, or simply not appreciated by the Prosecution. The plain language meaning and reading of the laws introduced into evidence does not support the claim of superior authority as to Sreten Lukic, and in fact neither does the other evidence adduced. If one looks at the evidence adduced, it is plain that Sreten Lukic did not, in fact, have effective control over all MUP units, as the Prosecution alleges at paragraphs 66 and 67 of the indictment. Likewise, no evidence was adduced that Lukic planned, organised, coordinated, or controlled all MUP forces alleged at paragraph 15 of the indictment. Likewise, there is no evidence showing how he could have control over non-MUP units. Now, if we look at the allegations of the indictment, we have to clarify one other matter arising from paragraph 7. At paragraph 7 it is stated that in May of 1998 Lukic ascended to the position of head of the MUP staff. No other evidence was adduced to prove this; rather, Exhibit P1505, as well as the live testimony of Witness Ljubinko Cvetic, established that Lukic came to this position within the MUP staff on the 11th of June, 1998. Now, although the OTP in its submission will likely point to Exhibit P1505 as supporting their claim that Lukic had control and command over the RDB, that is the state security units, as well as the RJB, the public security units, primarily because Mr. Gajic of the RDB is listed as assistant head of the staff, all the evidence adduced runs counter to this showing the way that the decision was implemented in the field. A host of witnesses including the aforementioned Ljubinko Cvetic, Shaun Byrnes, General DZ, Colonel Richard Ciaglinski, Colonel Maisonneuve, Colonel Phillips, and Colonel Loncar testified and established that Gajic of the DB was not, in fact, Lukic's assistant, but rather Colonel Mijatovic held that position in practice. Likewise, Cvetic, when asked to identify the members of the MUP staff, did not name any of the other persons set forth in P1505. So there has not been evidence proving that the DB fell under Mr. Lukic's control. What about the other units? Ljubinko Cvetic clearly enunciated that the SAJ and the JSO were directly subordinated to the chiefs of the RJB and the RDB respectively, which of course means they could not be subordinated to Mr. Lukic. We heard testimony from a former member of the PJP, K25, who also confirmed that the JSO was subordinated to the RDB and had a chain of command apart from the RJB. This is at transcript page 4722, line 20, through transcript page 4723, line 6. P1505 also sets forth the narrower empowerment of the MUP staff of Kosovo, which again the Prosecution has ignored. K25 further testified about the overall commander of the PJP units as being someone other than Lukic. He identified Obrad Stevanovic at transcript page 4732, line 12. This evidence was corroborated by another former PJP member, K79, who stated explicitly that: "Your Honour, my commander had meetings with Obrad Stevanovic, the commander of the PJP units. Mr. Lukic was not the commander of the PJP units and I don't see why they would have to meet." Transcript page 9622, lines 11 through 13. The evidence is also clear through other witnesses that General Stevanovic, assistant minister of the Ministry of Internal Affairs was on the ground continuously throughout the relevant time-period of the indictment. Now, with respect to the SUPs, the Secretariats of Internal Affairs, Prosecution Exhibit P1074, a work-plan for the year 1999 of the Pristina Secretariat of the Interior, does not mention the MUP staff as having any role in its functioning and, rather, states that its functioning was controlled by the RJB of the ministry in Belgrade. Indeed, the first words of this exhibit are: "On the bases of the programme of work of the RJB of the MUP of Serbia for the year 1999 ..." And so forth. Clearly the RJB and the minister -- ministry in Belgrade are the organs that planned the work of the SUPs as well. With respect to OPGs, the Operative Sweep Groups that were discussed as a MUP unit, Witness K86, another MUP insider witness, trumpeted by the Prosecution as a key witness in their case, testified that these units were actually commanded by the SUP chiefs themselves. Transcript page 7353, lines 3 through 9. Exhibits P1247 and P1249 likewise show that the commander of the PJP at the SUP level was also the commander of the OPG and that the OPG were actually a component of the PJP, meaning that their chain of command would be as the other witnesses testified to, not going to Sreten Lukic. Accordingly, despite calling a number of MUP insider witnesses, the existence of an actual superior/subordinate relationship between Lukic and the various MUP units and organs in the field has not been proven. Further, Ljubinko Cvetic, one of these insiders, testified that the MUP staff in Pristina, and indeed Sreten Lukic, had no role or power or authority to discipline any employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and that such a role was played directly by the minister and other authorities in Belgrade. This is from transcript page 8155, lines 4 through 19, and it is also demonstrated by Exhibit 6D133 which shows that the MUP staff was bypassed and had no role in disciplining MUP personnel. I would remind the Court that Judge Bonomy pressed this point with Witness Cvetic, who remained steadfast that it was very clearly explained that the staff and Lukic had no authority whatsoever to punish members of the MUP. Accordingly, a fundamental requirement to be considered a superior within the three-pronged test, the power to discipline an alleged subordinate, cannot be satisfied by the evidence adduced and Article 7(3) liability cannot attach to Mr. Lukic, and as such should be stricken. Now, just for the record, the last prong that the alleged superior knew of the actions of his alleged subordinates, none of the evidence has established that any crimes were reported to the MUP staff from the field. Indeed, the minutes of meetings of the MUP staff that were introduced into evidence, I have some numbers here, I believe P1990 and P1993 demonstrated that crimes alleged in the indictment were not discussed or known of. Likewise, no orders were given by anyone to commit criminal acts. The MUP staff daily reports introduced into evidence - and I urge the Chamber to review them all - likewise demonstrate the type of information available to the MUP staff which should not include knowledge or reporting of any criminal wrong-doing in the field. On the issue of knowledge or notice, it should be recalled that the oft-cited General Vasiljevic, a high-ranking official in the security organ of the VJ who was tasked specifically with investigating crimes in Kosovo and who had security operatives giving him unverified hearsay information that they could not confirm, he even testified that he knew nothing and heard nothing about the alleged crimes from this indictment from his operatives. Now, if Vasiljevic, who as we saw, was keen to take issue with the MUP and accuse the MUP, perhaps due to his personal contacts with the RDB, but if he who had operatives in Djakovica and elsewhere didn't know about the alleged killings in Meja, Korenica, and elsewhere, how is it expected or believed that Sreten Lukic would know if such crimes were not reported to him either? Again, I stress, no evidence was presented establishing that Lukic knew or that these crimes were reported to him at the relevant time-period of 1999? On knowledge: K25, who spent four days at Mala Krusa expressed surprise of the alleged killing and burning of over 100 persons that was said to have occurred precisely during this time-period. He didn't know anything about it, despite having been on the ground. And again, there was no evidence that Sreten Lukic was ever on the ground. These are only examples. There is another example of what actions were taken when there was knowledge of killings. It should be recalled that two -- actually, three incidents that General Vasiljevic knew about were fully processed. The killings in Podujevo, Kosovska Mitrovica, and Kosovo Polje, although not in the indictment were known to Vasiljevic and through cross-examination it was determined and from the other evidence in the case it has been determined that the perpetrators were arrested and even though members of the MUP were arrested by the relevant MUP authorities and the MUP structures acted in accordance with the law and handed them over to the appropriate judicial authorities for processing. I must stress that if you review the law that has been presented, you will see that with respect to the functioning of the MUP this is all the police is empowered to do. They have no control over the functioning of the judiciary. It's not like the military that has their own judicial organs. The civilian organs of the judiciary have absolutely no connection with the police. Now, Article 7(1) liability that is alleged against Mr. Lukic, the same logic applies for Article 7(1) liability insofar as the evidence has failed to establish any involvement of Lukic in the crimes alleged. The specific instances of murder, for example, will be discussed later. In fact, there is only one witness who even mentioned Lukic within the context of any direct participation in any alleged activity, and that was Bozidar Protic in the context of claiming to have recognised Lukic's voice over the telephone as the one directing him to find corpses to be transferred to Serbia. However, the evidence of Protic, we submit, is incredulous and cannot be relied on at this stage due to its unbelievable nature. One would have to suspend belief to afford this evidence any credence and therefore it is not proper evidence to sustain a conviction or to survive 98 bis. First of all, if we are to believe Protic's initial testimony, he drove Lukic for six months as his personal driver and recognised the voice on the phone as being "assistant minister Lukic" because of this fact. Transcript page 11299 lines 20 through 25. However, at the relevant time-period, as the evidence showed, Sreten Lukic was not an assistant minister of the interior and only became so under the democratic government that overthrew Slobodan Milosevic. Now Protic later conceded that he, in fact, had driven Lukic only a handful of occasions, once in Kosovo in 1990 and one or two times in Belgrade to his home, a full 8 to 10 years before hearing the voice on the telephone that he immediately recognised. Protic's evidence also runs counter to the sworn statements that that he gave to the MUP Working Group in 2001 and also to the sworn testimony he gave the Belgrade investigative judge, Dilparic, in 2003. Protic, when he came here, claimed that during the 2001 statement he was fearful for repercussions if he mentioned Lukic because of the way that he had been summarily retired and the fact that he still had family members who still worked in the ministry and could be dealt with similarly. However, the evidence demonstrated that, in fact, the 2001 statement was taken long before any of the retirement proceedings occurred relative to Protic and that he actually had no such fear at the time. We see this from transcript page 11353, line 21, through 11354, line 9. Remarkably yet another inconsistency within the sworn statement initially given to Belgrade by Mr. Protic was that the person on the other end of the line called him by his first name. And then in his testimony before this Trial Chamber that changed to the person calling him by his family name, transcript page 11311, line 23, to 11312, line 1. Additionally, Protic did concede another telling fact, that he had once gone to Lukic when Lukic was chief of the RJB after the Kosovo conflict and had asked for Lukic to illegally give him an apartment or flat, which Lukic refused to do. This animosity over Lukic's refusal to breach the law to give Protic a flat can be seen as another reason for the change and the unbelievable testimony of Protic. Lastly on Protic, the testimony runs afoul of the testimony we heard at this Tribunal from three other witnesses and contained in the multiple statements tendered through K84 that demonstrate -- that clearly do not reference Sreten Lukic as having any role in the clandestine transport of bodies to Serbia. Thus, as this unbelievable evidence is the sole evidence presented by the Prosecution linking Sreten Lukic personally to the commission or covering up of crimes, it alone is not sufficient to establish his guilt and acquittal ought to be granted. At paragraph 24 of the indictment, the Prosecution alleges the creation of the Joint Command as being in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise, in that it had de facto command authority over both VJ and MUP units. The importance of the Joint Command to the Prosecution's case was highlighted by the opening statement of Mr. Hannis when he stated: "The Joint Command was closely involved in the planning, execution, and monitoring of the various combat operations in Kosovo during the first half of 1999. In effect, the Joint Command brought together the two separate chains of command of the VJ and the MUP." This is transcript page 445, line 4 through 7. However, the evidence adduced at trial failed to demonstrate the Joint Command to be anything nearly as nefarious as suggested by the Prosecution. As my colleagues have pointed out already, the Joint Command documents are merely documents of the Pristina Corps, issuing orders to VJ units. Not a single Joint Command document in evidence purports to issue orders to MUP units. Indeed, MUP insider Ljubinko Cvetic essentially debunked the Prosecution's case on the Joint Command in answering Judge Bonomy's question that: "If I could also ask you, you've given evidence already that the normal chain of command according to the Law of the Interior was in place for both the MUP and the VJ throughout 1998. Now, the Joint Command, you've told us earlier, had been established by July 1998. Are you saying that with it in place the normal chains of command continued to operate?" The witness through interpretation answered: "Yes." This is from 8 December 2006 transcript, page 8123, lines 6 through 12. Another vaunted insider witness Mr. Vasiljevic produced a notebook entry for what he called a Joint Command meeting which turned out to be an innocuous meeting at the Pristina Corps headquarters, Exhibit P2532. Now, even the purported minutes of the Joint Command P1468, whose dubious authenticity we must accept for purposes of Rule 98 bis, do not set forth any orders to commit crimes nor any other activities that could be deemed to be criminal nature. Crucially no documents set forth any type of plan to deport Albanian civilians from Kosovo and Metohija. And within the "Joint Command" itself, it ought to be recalled that Vasiljevic, albeit only after being confronted with the videotape of his words in his interview with the Prosecution, testified that among the several participants, including MUP participants, Lukic had the least significant standing, being as he was the last hole on the flute. Transcript page 9066, lines 8 through 10. Now, apart from this, we had very little evidence about the functioning of the MUP during the period of the NATO bombing, that is the critical time-period of the indictment. For instance, Shaun Byrnes confirmed he did not know how the MUP functioned during that time-period or even who the most senior MUP officers on the ground were during that time and how they functioned. Transcript page 12230, lines 10 through 15. Similarly, all the Kosovo Verification Mission witnesses confirmed that their information only related to the time-period prior to the NATO bombings. Again, I cannot stress greatly enough that the Prosecution failed to call an expert on the structure and functioning of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Based on the paucity of this evidence, there is no way that a conviction of Sreten Lukic can be established, relative to any purported command authority arising out of this so-called Joint Command or otherwise. Now, if we can turn to some of the specific allegations of the indictment as to crimes, I would just like to highlight how flat the Prosecution case has fallen, particularly with respect to the allegations that had been made previously about the participation of MUP personnel. And again, I'll only highlight some of the murders for sake of efficiency. The indictment specifies 11 incidents of murder, while three incidents have been removed from the indictment by order of the Trial Chamber, the evidence presented relating to the others at this stage can be said to establish that certain crimes were committed by certain individuals; however, it cannot be said that these crimes have been linked via nexus to Sreten Lukic either by way of knowledge, plan, order, effective control, meaningful contribution, or assistance. Indeed, the evidence has shown that these regrettable crimes have been shown to be private crimes committed by private individuals for very personal reasons, and that -- although some of the individuals were police members or MUP members, they were acting on their own, outside of the orders and directives given to them. Other incidents were committed apparently by unknown individuals and so far as the Prosecution has seen fit not to investigate and present evidence differentiating between paramilitary, army, police, civilians or otherwise, the true identity of the perpetrators cannot be established. Although it is respectfully submitted that the Prosecution case has failed to establish the necessary evidence for criminal liability on any of the murders, we will look through them in greater detail. The first such example would be the incident in Suva Reka, the Berisha family killings. The Prosecution trumpeted this event as having been planned and ordered by MUP superior officers in Suva Reka and carried out by MUP subordinate officers. Transcript page 3990, line 14, as well as transcript page 4005, lines 10 through 11. Clearly this was not something that was part of their duties. Again, the perpetrators of the crimes are neighbours, locals. And we heard testimony from various of the victim's family that they saw the perpetrators consuming alcohol and found evidence of drug use prior to undertaking the heinous acts alleged. Likewise, the Prosecution introduced evidence relative to the alleged perpetrators, the names of individuals stated to have been involved in the killings. The investigations of the Prosecution revealed that very few of the perpetrators had any formal connection to the Serbian MUP. I would draw the Court's attention to Exhibits P2335, P2849, P2850, and P2851, for instance. One of the Nikolic men who was a firefighter within the MUP was not even listed on the guard rosters that were introduced into evidence through Witness Sweeney, so it cannot established that those that were formerly affiliated with the local SUP in Prizren in any way actually took place -- took part in the activities as part of their official duties. Indeed there was evidence of another plausible explanation for this event; namely, it was adduced in evidence that other members of the Nikolic family had been previously abducted from Mala Krusa by the KLA and had been mistreated by the KLA. I refer, for instance, to transcript page 4403 through 4404. Accordingly, private vendetta or revenge by the Nikolic clan against the local Albanians cannot be ruled out, particularly insofar as the vast majority of the alleged perpetrators that were named by the witnesses have been determined not to have ever been members of the MUP. Now, again with respect to the Meja and Korenica in Djakovica, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the VJ security officer who was investigating allegations of crimes in Kosovo, testified that his operative from Djakovica gave him information, including about other locales such as Kosovska Mitrovica. However, it is crucial to note what his security organ failed to tell him. Vasiljevic denied having any information about Meja and Korenica -- there's no reference to Meja or Korenica or the events there, even though it is within the geographic backyard of his security operative and despite the fact that the other witness, Nike Peraj, identified this same security operative, individual, as being an eye-witness with him to bodies. Accordingly either Nike Peraj cannot be fully believed or the locals in Djakovica, including Vasiljevic's security organ were hiding the crimes even from their superiors; thus, there's no way that Lukic would be privy to this information, if indeed it was hidden from him. Now, the same is true for incidents -- there's another factor that needs to be examined with respect to incidents relating to the deportation, alleged forcible transfer, and alleged persecution that we have heard, alleged -- that we've heard about. Bislim Zyrapi, as we have heard from the submissions of my colleagues, testified that the KLA had a policy of ordering civilians to vacate villages and go along with them as part of their battle strategy.
