I would be remiss at this point if I did not mention one other element that needs to be understood to gain an understanding of the situation on the ground during the time-period of the indictment. The activities of the OVK, the UCK, the KLA, and others. We heard references throughout, in the testimony of Mr. Abrahams, for instance, and within the testimony of Mr. Shaun Byrnes, about the organisation calling itself the FARK, the -- FARK, F-A-R-K, Armed Forces of the Republic of Kosova, who engaged in activities. Mr. Byrnes said that they were blamed by the KLA for the bombing of the Panda Bar in Pec that were on the ground at the same time and engaging in conflict with the KLA supporters. Likewise, Mr. Byrnes, at transcript page 12241, lines 5 through 24, testified about activities of the UCK-KLA in abducting and mistreating LDK supporters, that is to say, supporters of Mr. Rugova's party. And indeed we did have testimony from other witnesses about persons that were arrested by the KLA who were ethnic Albanians from rival political factions. We also have to take into account the movement of the KLA into the urban sector and the urban fighting that took place that Mr. Phillips, for instance, confirmed and testified as to. The Ministry of Interior throughout all this had, therefore, multiple enemies that it was confronted with. On the one hand, it had multiple groups of armed ethnic Albanian insurgents, terrorists, drug smugglers, criminals, as we heard Shaun Byrnes testify to; on the other hand, it had NATO, which was causing a threat from the sky and the ever-present threat of land troops; and you had a third enemy: Criminals of all ethnicities who were operating on the ground and, indeed, the evidence shows that despite the situations the MUP operated to uphold laws and arrest perpetrators of crimes, whoever they were. This brings us to the issue of volunteers that is alleged and is one of the cornerstones of the Prosecution case in the indictment, the alleged incorporation of volunteers into the MUP, the so-called Skorpions, the Arkan people. We heard from Witness Stoparic that, in fact, the Skorpions were a legitimate reserve -- were legitimate reserve members of the SAJ Police Unit. Accordingly, there can be nothing inherently illegitimate read into their deployment. Further, as Stoparic made clear, the killings in Podujevo by members of this reserve SAJ force were not ordered, instigated, nor condoned by the police superiors present. And while the perpetrators and their entire unit were verbally reprimanded and physically sent away from Kosovo, police officers tended to the victims and even saved a baby from one of the bodies. The evidence likewise was clear through Witness Stoparic that the perpetrators eventually were arrested and processed, leading to court convictions. There is no evidence that Lukic was involved in the deployment of this unit, but it should be pointed out that even Vasiljevic in his testimony could not identify any other alleged crimes committed by this unit following the reprimand, following the arrest of the perpetrators and their redeployment into Kosovo. Now, with respect to Arkan's men, the only evidence of note in this regard is Vasiljevic again, who makes it clear and claims that he was told by Rade Markovic that he had deployed a handful of men to Kosovo under the RDB structure, again reserve JSO. Vasiljevic could point to no known crime committed by the men, save the ordinary murders that the evidence showed had been committed in Kosovska Mitrovica by reserve JSO member Veselinovic who likewise was immediately arrested and processed and convicted by the Serb authorities, despite being a member of the RDB and JSO. Again as it was a DB unit there is no evidence of Lukic being aware or otherwise involved in the deployment. Now, if we move to 1998 -- and I believe, Your Honours, are we close to the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is a very good time to break, Mr. Ivetic. So we'll adjourn now and resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue with my submissions, I do have one correction for the transcript. At page 58 of today's transcript, line 2, I misquoted the transcript page I was referring to from the Protic testimony. The correct citation should be the transcript page 11399, not 299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I will embark on the final portion of my submissions. I would just like to comment upon the allegations within the indictment which repeatedly refer to my client's alleged knowledge of crimes in 1998 conducted by MUP and other personnel. However, the evidence on the record clearly established, as I've repeatedly said, that Lukic did not come to his position at the MUP staff in Pristina until June the 11th of 1998, thus his knowledge of events in Kosovo can only flow from that date forward. I would remind the Court that as the allegations in the indictment even set forth, Lukic was at the city SUP in Belgrade from 1992 onwards through his -- through June of 1998. The only real event in 1998 that could perhaps fall under the penumbra of the Prosecution's assertions would be the Gornje Obrinje event, but we've already heard testimony from various witnesses including Jan Kickert at transcript page 11226, line 21, through 11227, line 14, about the various efforts undertaken to investigate that event by the Serbian authorities which were unsuccessful because of attacks and threats from the UCK-KLA that held a base near Gornje Obrinje, and in fact we did hear about a -- I believe it was a Red Cross vehicle that had been destroyed by a KLA mine in that -- on that same road just a few days prior to the attempted investigation. So it must be stressed that the only evidence on record of any type of events from 1998 that are enumerated in the indictment would be this Gornje Obrinje that shows that the authorities did attempt to undertake investigations and therefore, again, there's not this nefarious undertone of doing nothing on the part of the police. Lastly I would just point out that there are, I believe, in my submission, portions of the indictment for which not a single witness, proper witness, was called and off the top of my head I can recite -- there was a reference to a mosque in Brestovac for which not a single witness was called save for Mr. Riedlmayer to say the mosque was damaged. There was not a witness provided for how the mosque was damaged. I believe that's true for all the cultural monuments that were alleged to have been damaged. And I believe that there are some sites that are on the indictment for which not a single witness was called as well; the village of Vojnike comes to mind as one of those. I believe there are several more but in any event it's something that the Chamber should look at to ensure that the Prosecution has actually called witnesses for everything that is alleged in the indictment, as I submit they have not. So respectfully, Your Honours, the evidence, all the evidence, not just those dramatic examples I have highlighted here, when viewed in the light of Rule 98 bis does not, respectfully, stand the test and does not meet the Prosecution's burden of establishing a credible case against Mr. Lukic for him to answer. Accordingly, the Lukic Defence would request an acquittal of all counts directed against him. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Hannis, before you start your submissions, are there any revisals to the indictment that you have to propose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any at this time. We have looked at particular lines in the crime base, but we had come to the conclusion that there was some evidence regarding those. There might have been one or two where there was a question about the wording of whether it was a shelling or an aerial bombing or there was a question about whether three villages named were correctly identified. But because we were focusing at this stage on counts, I don't have any specific unproven allegation to give to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us an indication of how you intend to go about responding then, Mr. Hannis. Have you a pattern to this response? Are you going to take them accused by accused or are you going to take it count by count or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I intended to address that first thing in my comments to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It really is an honour for me to address Your Honours at this point. For a fellow who started his prosecutorial career in a little town in Arizona doing speeding tickets and DWIs to speak to Your Honours at the International Tribunal for war crimes is a privilege. Both Mr. Stamp and I will be addressing you, Your Honours. I'm going to go first. I'm going to address the following matters: I'm going to speak, first of all, about the 98 bis standard, give you a very brief overview of the counts in this case; I'll talk about the joint criminal enterprise, as we've alleged it; In connection with that, I'll discuss a little bit about the Joint Command; I'll talk about Article 7(1) responsibility in general; I'll talk about the crime base; and I'll speak specifically about three of the accused are military accused General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, and General Lazarevic; and I'm just going to speak one time so we won't be popping up back and forth. When I'm done sometime tomorrow, Mr. Stamp will address the issues of Article 7(3) responsibility in general and the lack of punishment. He's talk about the bodies evidence. He'll talk about the other three accused, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Lukic. Thank you. Now, one thing that we are in general agreement with our learned friends about is the standard of Rule 98 bis. The rule, as you know, was changed in 2004 and now the focus is on counts rather than charges. The standard to be applied in respect of each of the five counts in this indictment which are deportation; forcible transfer; murder, two different ways, murder as a crime against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war; and persecutions. The standard is whether there is evidence on record which, if accepted, if believed by you and taken at its highest could lead a reasonable trier of fact to be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charges. At this stage the question is not whether there's evidence contrary to the Prosecution's case on record. And we've heard a lot of talk about that but that's not the standard at this stage. The Trial Chamber is: "Required to assume that the Prosecution's evidence was entitled to credence unless incapable of belief." And I'm quoting from the Jelesic case from the appeal judgement of 5 July 2001. At this stage of the proceedings, it's not the task of Your Honours to make assessments of credibility of witnesses, to weigh the evidence, or to resolve conflicts or inconsistencies in the evidence. As I said before, the only exception is for evidence so inherently incredible that no reasonable fact-finder can rely on it. And we say there is no such evidence relied upon by us to support the five counts at issue. In other words, all evidence that's not inherently incredible should be viewed in the light most favourable to the Prosecution. Based on that standard, we say there's more than ample evidence in the case from which a reasonable Trial Chamber could find each and all of the accused guilty of all five counts beyond a reasonable doubt. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move from that subject I have just one question I want to have your comment on. The Defence also rely, so far as the case depends, on circumstantial evidence on the -- the apparent rule that we have that before there can be a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, guilt must be the only reasonable interpretation of the evidence. So in other words, if there's another reasonable interpretation, a finding of guilt can't be made. Do you see that also as a matter for the Trial Chamber at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. Because at this point the question is whether a reasonable Trial Chamber could find based on this evidence. And so I guess my argument at this point if it would be reasonable to conclude from that evidence, maybe not the only reasonable conclusion but it would be a reasonable conclusion that at this point we can proceed on. You don't have to find it's the only reasonable conclusion at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regard to the charges in the indictment, as you know, Your Honours, this case we've said from the beginning is principally a case about deportation. Our principal submission regarding that is that the crimes charged in the indictment were committed pursuant to a common plan, a design, or purpose. It was a joint criminal enterprise to which these accused were a part. They were members of that joint criminal enterprise. Now, you've heard much argument about the fact that there is no document, there is no plan, but I submit to you you shouldn't expect one. Since the Nuremberg trials after World War II, I think anyone who's likely to engage in war crimes was not likely to put it down in writing anymore. It's not the kind of thing that people will sit around and brag about or write about. And it is something that, we say, is shown by all kinds of evidence. I'll go through that in a moment. There are three prongs to our argument in this regard. First, we say there is ample evidence at this stage from dozens of eye-witnesses and dozens more who have second-hand evidence about the crimes charged that they, indeed, were committed. We have bodies, murders were committed, we have dozens of eye-witnesses who themselves were deported and have come to court and told you about that. Second, we say that it's clear from the scope and the nature of these crimes committed in Kosovo that they weren't random acts. It wasn't a matter of serendipity that these same kinds of crimes were happening in location after location throughout Kosovo at and around the same time. Rather, they were committed pursuant to a common plan, design, or purpose: A joint criminal enterprise. When these crimes are placed in the relevant context, we say there's ample other evidence to prove that they were part of a joint criminal enterprise, and that joint criminal enterprise had as its purpose to alter the ethnic balance in Kosovo so that the Serbs could remain in control of that province. Thirdly, there is evidence that each and all of the accused contributed to the execution of that joint criminal enterprise and that they intended to further the aims of that joint criminal enterprise. I'm going to talk about some of those issues in detail in a minute, but I want to mention some very recent legal developments. I think Mr. Ackerman made reference to the Brdjanin case, as well he might, and in light of that we feel our case can be somewhat narrow with regard to the JCE. And after I speak to that, Your Honour, I'm going to set out our position that even if you were to find that there's no evidence that a reasonable Trial Chamber could accept that each of these accused participated in the joint criminal enterprise, we are then going to ask you to find that they are responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) for ordering, planning, instigating, or otherwise aiding and abetting the crimes charged in the indictment; and alternatively, pursuant to Article 7(3), for their failure to prevent the crimes from happening and/or to punish the perpetrators of the crimes. And in regard to that, Your Honour, I might note one other matter regarding 98 bis and the standard at this stage of the proceedings. Two recent cases have noted that the amended version of Rule 98 bis: "Does not require evidence capable of establishing each and every allegation or form of liability, that is criminal responsibility, pleaded in respect of a count to support a conviction on a count. The Prosecution need only ultimately succeed in proving one of the forms of criminal responsibility it relies on for there to be a conviction on a count." The quote is from Judge Moloto in the Martic decision on the 3rd of July, 2006, at pages 5960 and 5961 of the transcript in that case. And he was quoting from the earlier Mrksic Trial Chamber decision. And now I would like to address briefly the scope of our JCE allegations following the Brdjanin appeal judgement from the 3rd of April of this year. In Brdjanin, as Your Honours are aware, the Trial Chamber -- the Prosecution alleged the Trial Chamber had erred in law, in holding that persons who carry out the actus reus, the hands-on perpetrators of the crimes, had to be members of the JCE. The Appeals Chamber granted that ground of appeal, and in so doing they adopted, Your Honour, a portion of Judge Bonomy's separate opinion in the decision on General Ojdanic's motion challenging jurisdiction previously filed in this very case. The Appeals Chambers held that what matters is not whether the person carrying out the actus reus, the physical perpetrator, was a member of the JCE, but whether the crime in question was a part of the common purpose. The person carrying out the actus reus need not know of the JCE, but if there's evidence that they had such knowledge it could be a factor in deciding whether the crimes form part of the common criminal purpose. To hold a member of the JCE responsible for crimes committed by persons who were not members of the JCE, it has to be shown that the crime can be imputed to a member of the JCE and that the member acted in accordance with the common plan. What we have to do is establish a link between the crime and the member of the JCE, and it's a matter that is to be assessed on a case-by-case basis depending on the particular facts in that case. And frankly, Your Honour, we think that's a very logical common sense approach to dealing with these kinds of crimes. In modern war, as Mr. Ackerman talked about, these kind of crimes carried on such a grand scale over such a large amount of territory to try and say that the foot soldier on the ground with a rifle is in some sort of agreement or common enterprise with the president of a country we think is contrary to common sense. When the accused or any other members of the JCE in order to further the common criminal purpose, which here we say was to alter the ethnic balance in Kosovo, to maintain Serbian control, they use a person or persons to carry out the physical perpetration, the actus reus of the crimes which form part of the common purpose; and those persons carry out some other crime or different crime, the members of the JCE are still responsible for those crimes. And in our context, Judge, I'm talking about murders because we say the primary plan was deportation; altering the ethnic balance by getting these people out. But if in the course of doing that they commit murders, we say that the members of the JCE can be responsible if those murders were, number one, reasonably foreseeable that they might be perpetrated by one or more of the persons being used to carry out the deportations forming part of the common purpose; and number two, that the accused willingly took that risk. In this context, willingly taking the risk means that the accused acted with the awareness that such a crime was a possible consequence of implementing the enterprise and they decided to continue in the enterprise. Paragraph 20 of our indictment, Your Honours, sets out that there was a JCE in which these six were members. We pled our JCE 1 in two alternative formulations. In the first we allege that the members of the JCE were the accused, other named individuals, including Rade Markovic and: "Unidentified persons who were members of the command and coordinating bodies and members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia." Alternatively, we allege in our indictment, that the accused and other named individuals were members of the JCE and that they "implemented the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise through members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia whom they controlled to carry out the crimes charged in the indictment." In light of the appeals judgement in Brdjanin, Your Honours, we intend now to only proceed on the basis of that alternative articulation, that these six members of the JCE used members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia that they had control over to carry out the deportations, forced transfers, murders, and persecutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you opened this part of your submission and referred to what Mr. Ackerman said, you gave me the impression that somehow or other Brdjanin had made your task more difficult, at least that's what you were going to say, but is it not, in fact, the opposite?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I think it makes our task easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But to avoid any misunderstandings we are maintaining our other submissions regarding the JCE, Your Honour, including the alternative allegation in paragraph 21 where we say with regard to the crimes charged in Counts 3 through 5, that is, murder the two ways and persecutions, were natural and foreseeable consequences of the deportations and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the third version of JCE?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's JCE 3 and that's an alternative force that we still are relying on. Now, with regard to JCE 1, I think Mr. Ackerman made reference to this, regarding the actus reus of JCE we need to show, first of all, that there were a plurality of persons involved in the commission of the crime that is accused; number two, that they acted on the basis of a common plan, design, or purpose which amounted to or involved the commission of a crime provided for in the Statute, and maintaining control through altering the ethnic balance involved the commission of deportations and forcible transfers in this case; and that one or several of the co-perpetrators used the physical perpetrators to carry out the crimes. Those co-perpetrators controlled organised structures of power and used its members as tools. And we're referring primarily there to the VJ and the MUP. And then the accused participated in this common design, either physically or through the use of others. In real life, in the real world, Your Honour, one of the other JCE members named in our indictment is Slobodan Milosevic and in this JCE that we've alleged he's in some way the sun around which these other planets revolve. But they're all members of the JCE, they all had separate and distinctive roles to play and separate and distinctive contributions that they make which we'll discuss in more detail when we talk about each of the individual accused. Mr. Milutinovic was president of Serbia, he had previously been a foreign minister, had lots of previous dealings with internationals, and he was the face man in many aspects of this case who was put forward to deal with internationals. Mr. Sainovic was the point man in Kosovo and he was the hands-on political member in Kosovo coordinating the activities of the joint criminal enterprise. General Ojdanic, Pavkovic, and Lazarevic were those members who had control over the VJ and subordinate forces that carried out many of the physical acts on the ground. And Mr. Lukic from the MUP, who did the same thing in regard to police activities. We also need to show that the accused intended to perpetrate the crime, this being the shared intent on the part of the co-perpetrators, and we'll talk about evidence showing intent in a moment. I do want to talk about the general evidence that supports our claim that there was a joint criminal enterprise, that there was a common plan or purpose in which they shared. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence about how more than 800.000 Kosovo Albanians were deported to other countries, thousands were killed, Kosovo Albanian property was looted, dwellings and mosques were burned and destroyed, and countless people were beaten, intimidated, many women were raped, all as part of this campaign which was designed, we say, to alter the ethnic balance in Kosovo by removing substantial members of the Kosovo Albanians. These crimes primarily began within days of the first NATO bombings on 24 March 1999 in what we say was a systematic fashion all over Kosovo. These widespread synchronised crimes all across the province followed very similar patterns, and we say that in itself is some evidence that a Trial Chamber could accept as proof that they were committed pursuant to a common plan, design, or purpose. Mr. Ackerman yesterday made reference to the 13 Joint Command orders that are in evidence in this case, and at the end of the case we'll hope to do this. If you sit down and read those Joint Command orders identifying what forces are to engage in combat operations in what areas and on what dates, you will see that they closely reflect our crime sites and where people fled from, were driven out of, and where the killings occurred. The sheer scale of these deportations, because you've heard some evidence about the population and how many people actually lived in Kosovo at the time, the sheer scale suggests that they must have been the result of a plan or a design or a purpose. In that regard we refer you to Exhibit P2229, the statement of Fred Abrahams; P2438 and the attachment C to that statement which is P738 of a member of an international humanitarian organisation, which show that the number of refugees were around 850.000 by June of 1999. Patrick Ball's report concludes that the refugees in Kosovo had not left randomly. We say a Trial Chamber could on such evidence find that the reason the refugees left Kosovo was that they were forced to leave by the forces of FRY and Serbia. That's not the only evidence you have about that. You have the statements of many of the deportees themselves, the victims of these crimes. One that I think you'll probably remember was Sadije Sediku, she was the young woman who appeared before you here in a wheelchair. She and her family lived in the area near Kosovska Mitrovica and she told you how on the 14th of April police came to their home and told them they had to leave immediately. They were forced out. They travelled long distances across Kosovo to the west. Eventually the police told them to stay in another abandoned village, where they stayed for several days before Ms. Sediku was shot by who she says were police, Serbian police, that was the injury that caused her to end up in the wheelchair that she was in when she testified, and that happened on the 6th of May. You heard several similar accounts -- and then eventually with her wound in the back of a wagon behind a tractor she and her family were forced to go to Albania. You heard several similar accounts from other witnesses Dr. Gerxhaliu in Vucitrn, Edison Zatriqi from Pec, (redacted) (redacted), Halit Berisha from Suva Reka, all of whom told you that they were forced to leave their homes between, the 24 and 28 March, in the first four days of the war. Later in April, you had witnesses Lizane Malaj, Merita Deda from the Korenica-Guska-Meja area who said tell you about how they were forced out of their homes when police and military came to their village, shot and killed some of their family members, and told them to leave to go to Albania. Your Honours could also make such a finding based on witnesses like Maisonneuve, who testified that he spoke to numerous refugees in Albania who had told him how they had been told to leave their houses on short notice by the Serbian authorities and Colonel Ciaglinski, who also was told similar accounts when he visited the border area, I believe in Macedonia. Other categories of evidence, Your Honours, which we say support the allegation of the JCE and the existence of a plan include some of the historical background in this case. You heard from Baton Haxhiu, Adnan Merovci. Think Veton Surroi talked about it a little bit as well, about what had been happening in Kosovo from the early 1980s and a long history of problems and unrest and what we say were ever harsher and more restrictive methods directed towards the Kosovo Albanians in Kosovo. And, we say, the evidence shows that those measures had not worked and in some ways they had backfired, that Mr. Rugova, who was head of the LDK party that came into existence and more moderate than some of his successors eventually lost his leading position, in part I think because of a lack of success in reaching any kind of progress and more violent, more aggressive elements in Kosovo came into being. It seemed the harder that Serbs pushed, the worse the problem got. We say that is some evidence of why you can find that there was a plan. It was frustration, we say, on the part of Slobodan Milosevic and his colleagues with not being able to resolve the problem, being under intensive international pressure about how they were trying to solve the problem. And we say that's part of what led to this solution, the solution that Mr. Milosevic made reference to in October 1998 in the meeting with General Clark and General Naumann where he said, We'll find a solution for this problem in spring of 1999. Now, before the NATO bombing we have statements of several Serbs which we say reflect on the issue of a plan and the existence of joint criminal enterprise. Baton Haxhiu tells you that in 1997 he was at a meeting where he got information from a Serb in the security service that they had a scorched-earth plan for Kosovo. Mr. Ratomir Tanic told you how in the second half of 1997 he was told by Mr. Milosevic that the problem with the Kosovo Albanians was that they supported the KLA and that the problem was the number of Albanians, the sheer number, that had to be brought down to a reasonable figure. You also heard from Mr. Tanic, and I think it's also referred to in one of Mr. Petritsch's diplomatic cables, that in October 1998 Mr. Stambuk was saying that Yugoslavia, the FRY, wouldn't mind a few NATO bombs, that the bombing would be a good opportunity to cleanse the Albanians. This is from Mr. Tanic's testimony at transcript 6376 and in his statement, Exhibit 1D44, at paragraph 94. You also have evidence Mr. Naumann told us in his testimony in the Milosevic case at transcript 6989 to page 6991, which is in evidence as Exhibit P2512, that Milosevic told him and Clark that there were about 900.000 Albanians and about 600.000 other ethnic groups in Kosovo. That was quite different from the numbers that they were aware of from other sources. And in the context of this in his testimony in Milosevic, Mr. Naumann said Sainovic expressed concern about the reproduction rate of the Albanians. In October of 1998, Naumann told us about that meeting where Mr. Milosevic had his outburst after the signing of the October agreements and said a problem -- the Kosovo problem, a solution would be found in the spring of 1999 and it would be a final solution. It would do, as in 1946 in Drenica, which as Milosevic explained was getting them together and shooting them. Mr. Milutinovic at Rambouillet in February of 1999 made a statement that Mr. Petritsch recounted as him indicating that bombing by NATO, bombing of Serbia by NATO, would lead to massacres. And he understood that to mean massacres of Kosovo Albanians. And Exhibit P2307, which is the statement of protected witness K73, who told us that General Pavkovic told officers at a -- at a briefing or a meeting shortly before the war that as soon as the NATO bombs fall they would have to "clean their back from Albanians." We say all this is evidence that suggests that there was a plan to get rid of the problem, to get rid of the Kosovo Albanians by driving them out. Other evidence, we say, that supports this theory is the arming of Serbs and the disarming of Albanians that occurred prior to the conflict. Colonel Pesic, who testified at transcript page 7159, told us how Albanians were not called-up for the Territorial Defence, only Serbs were; he told us that when they learned that weapons no longer needed by their army had been distributed to civilians for their own protection, he agreed that most of those who had been so armed were only Serbs. And in Exhibit P1415 you have the June 1998 order for arming and formation of village defences in that regard. Pesic agreed that those armed were only Serbs. On the other side, Exhibit P1203 from 15 October 1998 talks about the continued MUP operations to collect weapons from Albanian villages. So at the same time the Serbs are being armed, the Kosovo Albanians are being disarmed. Other evidence, we say, supports our submission that there was a joint criminal enterprise being formed to carry out this common purpose or plan, the Joint Command. I want to talk a little bit about the Joint Command because everybody -- just about everybody's talked about the Joint Command and as I understood it from the Defence some seem to be suggesting still that there wasn't a Joint Command, at least not in 1999. And I think it's interesting, Your Honour, to look at why there is so much controversy about the Joint Command. We say it's clear from all the evidence and documents that you've now heard that there really isn't a serious question that there was a Joint Command in existence and functioning, not just in 1998 but in 1999. You'll remember Mr. Coo testified and one of the things he talked about was the efforts we had made to get documentation from Serbia about the Joint Command and the initial response, I believe he testified to, was that there was only a Joint Command in 1998, and we got, through General Pavkovic, the minutes of the Joint Command in 1998 between July and October 1998, but the position was there was no Joint Command in 1999. One of the exhibits that suggests that it did continue beyond October 1998 is Exhibit P2166. This is the minutes of the operations interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo, a meeting that was held on the 29th of October, 1998, the minutes are dated the 2nd of November. We talked a lot about that, but I would encourage Your Honours to take a close look at that document, read it thoroughly, it's very illustrative of what the Joint Command had been doing. Many of our accused were at that meeting. It was chaired by Mr. Milosevic, but Mr. Milutinovic was there, Mr. Sainovic was there, General Pavkovic was there, and General Lukic was there. General Ojdanic had not yet reached the position of Chief of Staff, so General Perisic is at the meeting. But there's great discussion of the work that the Joint Command has done earlier in 1998 to combat terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija and there's discussion about whether or not the Joint Command needs to continue to exist, should continue to exist, and the assessment that the group reaches is that it should. And we say the evidence clearly shows that it did. Mr. Cvetic testified at transcript page 8051 that the Joint Command was established in July 1998. He told you how that at a MUP staff meeting on the 10th of July it was announced to them that it had been created, it had been set up at the highest level, that it included Mr. Sainovic, it included Dusko Matkovic, Milomir Minic, Sreten Lukic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic from the TEC, and David Gajic from the Serbian MUP. Now, we know from General Vasiljevic that on the 1st of June he attended a meeting in Kosovo of the Joint Command, and he told you who attended the meeting. Mr. Lukic -- General Lukic was there and General Pavkovic was there, that the meeting was chaired by Mr. Sainovic. So between October -- November 2nd, 1998, from the minutes that say it should continue and the 1st of June, 1999, they are still meeting with many of the same individuals, according to General Vasiljevic. But that's not the only evidence you have about the existence of the Joint Command. We have, I think, the 13 Joint Command orders that Mr. Ackerman made reference to yesterday, and we urge you to look at those. They don't have a signature; they only have a typed stamp that says, "Joint Command." But if you'll look in the upper left where you see the information -- the date of the document, you'll also see the number that we had explained to us was an interior number, an internal number, for the agency that was putting out the document. It's a sequential number. The first number is the subject number or an -- and it's followed by a sequential number in the year in which it's issued. I think those documents that we have regarding Joint Command orders beginning around the 22nd of March, 1999, I think the first one is 455-56. So you'll wonder where are the first 55. We eventually did find the order 455-1, but that's an order signed by General Pavkovic in February 1999 which is in the form of a directive. It's about a 40-page document which is in the nature of a directive like you saw from General Perisic in the summer of 1998. We say this shows the planning in February. At the same time negotiations were going on in Rambouillet, that the army was preparing for what was likely to happen after that. And you'll see where those deployments are ordered. You'll see that they line up with where the crimes occurred once the bombing had started. We urge you to look closely at those orders. Part of the Defence position has been: Well, there was no Joint Command. And if there was, well, it wasn't a command, it was a coordinating body and it didn't order anybody to do anything. But you look at the orders themselves and they say, usually in the last paragraph, it says: These operations, those that are set forth in the order, it says these operations are to be commanded by the Joint Command. So it's not just a coordinating body. You'll see other references to the Joint Command in exhibits -- in documents from the -- from the Supreme Command Staff for one; suggestions from General Ojdanic and the Supreme Command, and he makes reference to a particular Joint Command order and makes suggestions to how the 3rd Army might want to make some adjustments to that order from the Joint Command. So General Ojdanic and the Supreme Command Staff are aware of the existence of the Joint Command and apparently satisfied with it. They're not saying, You should ignore what the Joint Command is telling you to do, just merely making suggestions. You also see a reference to it in a 25 May 1999 document from General Pavkovic. This relates to the issue of the subordination of the MUP, and in this document - I'm trying to find the number, Your Honour, I'll get that for you in a moment - in this document General Pavkovic is complaining that the subordination of the MUP that had been ordered by the Supreme Command Staff in -- around the 18th or 20th of April, 1999, had not been complied with, that the MUP was not subordinating itself, as had been ordered. And he is suggesting to the Supreme Command Staff that they take steps to either make that happen or otherwise let the command of MUP units revert to the MUP staff of Kosovo, that through the -- through the Joint Command, as has been done up to that date. So it's clear that the Joint Command was in existence and that it was more than a coordinating body. And the fact that everyone has worked very hard on the Defence side, we say, to distance themselves from that body suggests that it has more importance than they want you to know. We think it is the body that effectively ensured the coordination and the carrying out of the operations that were designed to effect the joint criminal enterprise and its objective of forcing out the Kosovo Albanians. And I'm reminded -- I apparently misspoke before when I referred to 455-1, it is General Lazarevic's command or the Pristina Corps who issued that order. I think I may have said General Pavkovic, and if I did, I misspoke. Other evidence regarding the existence of a plan and the existence of the JCE we say you can find from the creation -- or from the removal, I'm sorry, the removal and replacement of other individuals within the army and the MUP. I'm talking particularly about General Perisic and Jovica Stanisic and eventually General Dimitrijevic. As you know, General Perisic was the Chief of Staff of the VJ in 1998, but as early as the summer of 1998 we know that he was having some disagreements with Mr. Milosevic about how the VJ was being used in Kosovo. He, in his letter that's Exhibit 717 that he wrote in July of 1998, took issue with certain practices that have gone on. He made reference to certain individuals going around the chain of command. We think other evidence indicates that was General Pavkovic. And he complained about non-authorised persons controlling or directing the use of VJ units in Kosovo. We think the other evidence indicates that there was probably Mr. Sainovic. And he says that the army should not be used in these kind of operations, this interior fight against terrorism, unless one of the three extraordinary states was declared: A state of emergency, a state of imminent threat of war, or a state of war. And you'll see in some of the discussions of the VJ collegium and the Supreme Defence Council that one of the reasons for this was because of the international scrutiny that Serbia was under at the time. There had already been one UN resolution earlier in the year, there would be another one to follow before the end of the year, about the violence in Kosovo. And Perisic was asking that one of the states be declared so the army could be used that way. Perisic was still on the job in October 1998 when the meetings took place where General Clark and Naumann that led to the October agreements, but in an earlier meeting in October you'll recall that when General Naumann and General Clark complained to Mr. Milosevic about the use of the 211th Brigade in Kosovo, Mr. Milosevic said, No, no, there isn't any such unit and it's not in Kosovo and Mr. Perisic corrected him and pointed out that, yes, indeed there was and it was in Kosovo. We say that's another reason that led to the removal of Mr. Perisic. He was not in agreement with the position that Mr. Milosevic had and other more amenable persons were sought, we say, to be in that position so that the plan that Mr. Milosevic and others eventually agreed upon could be carried out. Related to that in late 1998 and early 1999, we say there were obstructions of negotiations. Mr. Tanic told you how that Milosevic negotiated but at the same time he was preparing for war. Mr. Petritsch told you at transcript page 10723 that Hill had a meeting with Milutinovic on the 18th of February, which was absolutely unproductive. Milutinovic is cited in the Austrian diplomatic dispatch at Exhibit 562 as being intransigent in attempting to protract the negotiations. Ambassador Vollebaek at transcript 9519 testified that between Rambouillet and Paris the Serbs toughened their line and weren't willing to negotiate. At the same time, we say, Serbs were preparing for a spring offensive, the very spring offensive that Mr. Milosevic had talked about in October 1998. Exhibit P2512 is the testimony of General Naumann in the Milosevic case. At transcript 6989 Naumann recalled Milosevic stating that they were going to take care of the problem in the spring. He also in his statement and referring to Exhibit P1767, he said: "Looking at the scale and the magnitude of the activities that took place in Kosovo during the spring of 1999, there would have had to have been months of preparation." He says: "This inference can be drawn because of the coordinated large-scale movement of forces that took place." This is consistent with, we say, the -- the order or the directive issued by General Lazarevic in February of 1999, and that order is Exhibit P2808. It's an order for breaking apart and destruction of the SDS in the region of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo. Right during the middle of the Rambouillet negotiations. You also have the evidence and testimony of Colonel Crosland at P2645, the testimony of Ciaglinski in Exhibit P2489, the evidence from General DZ, who all talk about what they saw as a build-up of Serb forces and the bringing in of new and better equipment, the higher-grade tanks, the number of Serb forces going from a deployment of three companies to 15 by the time that DZ left. Similarly, Adnan Merovci told us that the LD activists who were watching the activities at the time estimated that as many as 30.000 troops or 30.000 VJ and MUP had recently entered Kosovo during the time between October 1998 and March 1999. There's also the general pattern of crimes which we talked about before, but related to that there's one thing that we think is important for you to bear in mind as well. A number of crime base witnesses have told you about how when they were forced to leave Kosovo and as they were crossing the border or sometimes on their way from their home to the border, that their identity papers were taken away from them, sometimes torn up in front of them, other times burned in their presence, and the licence plates from their vehicles were removed. We say this was part of the bigger plan, not only to remove them but to be sure that they can't come back. We say the way this works is that these Albanians are forced to leave, and if after the conflict for some reason they try to come back they don't have any identity papers to confirm that they were originally from Serbia and from Kosovo and they could be refused admission. That would help achieve the desired aim of maintaining Serb control in the province because you could keep out those hundreds of thousands of Albanians that you physically forced out earlier. K89 told you that when his unit went up he was told by his major that, for one, not a single Albanian ear was to remain in Kosovo and that their identification papers were to be torn, so as to prevent them from coming back - precisely what we claim. So there is some evidence which you can rely on. That was at transcript page 9124. And Exhibit P2677, which is the testimony of protected witness K54, he was told by a soldier who had been present at the border crossing at Vrmice that the MUP confiscated the identification documents of Albanians and set the documents on fire, that they had orders to do so, so that in case those people came back they would have no proof of ever having lived in Kosovo. And some of that ID document testimony is corroborated by others, not just the crime base victims. Maisonneuve told us that he spoke to numerous refugees when he was head of the refugee task force in Albania and said they all told him they had been forced to leave by the Serbian authorities, and at the border their identity documents were confiscated and licence plates from their vehicles were removed. That's at transcript page 11086. Colonel Ciaglinski in Milosevic also observed people crossing the border into Macedonia and that he tells us in -- at transcript page 3215 that he was told by these people that there most of them had had their identity cards taken from them at the train station before they were forced to walk across into Macedonia. Ambassador Vollebaek, likewise, told you at transcript 9523 that he was at the border and met some refugees whose ID papers and licence plates were taken away and destroyed. This is also consistent and supportive of the findings of Patrick Ball in Exhibit 1509 in his report when trying to decide whether these people left because of NATO bombing, because of KLA activity, or because of actions of the Serb army and police. We're not saying that some of these people didn't leave because of the bombing, we're not saying that some of these people didn't leave their villages because they were told to do so by the KLA in some instances. But we're saying there is evidence upon which you could, as a reasonable trier of fact, find beyond a reasonable doubt that they left because of the violent actions and the force of the Serb police and VJ. Now, with regard to the purpose of this criminal enterprise we say all that evidence, each of the different categories, we say, could support your finding, but when you put them all together you have more than enough to meet the standard at this phase of the case where you're making a 98 bis determination. I'm sorry, Your Honour, may I have a moment. Related to my comments earlier about the Joint Command, there are two other bodies that I want to briefly mention that I think are important for your understanding about whether or not there was an existence of a joint criminal enterprise and the participation of individual accused therein. One issue was raised regarding the Supreme Defence Council and the Supreme Command. Mr. Stamp will talk some more about that in connection with his comments on Mr. Milutinovic, but we would note that there are a number of items in the evidence which rebut the Defence argument that there was no such body as the Supreme Command. One of those documents, Your Honour, is an interview of General Pavkovic, Exhibit 949, at page 26 of that interview, he's asked about the Supreme Defence Council, which he indicates is made up of the president of Yugoslavia and the presidents of the republican units and he indicates that is the body from the time of peace. And the Supreme Command is formed by including the adequate or relevant military personnel who perform their duties. So the following composition: It has Supreme Commander, also the head of the headquarters of the Supreme Command, and also it has assistants for different departments, like for morale, for security, et cetera. He says, when asked: "At what point was the Supreme Command come into effect?" He says: "The Supreme Command comes into effect when the war is declared." And that was immediately after the Federal Assembly declared the state of war he thinks on the 23rd or 24th of March. The investigator asked: "So was the president -- so the president was involved with the Supreme Command and the presidents of the republic as well. Is that correct?" General Pavkovic answers: "Yes." "Can you name the other two, please?" His answer: "Milutinovic and Djukanovic." The investigator asked: "Did they both participate actively in the Supreme Command?" Pavkovic answers: "I saw Milutinovic but not Djukanovic." So from one of our accused we have existence of the Supreme Command but in other documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to comment on the extent to which that can be used as evidence. Is it not evidence restricted to the case against Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that's on argument to be made. I know this exhibit was admitted purport to your order of October 10th, 2006. There was -- there was no limitation put on the evidence. I don't know what your ruling will be if there's a Defence argument about how it can be used. We say it certainly can be against General Pavkovic because we say because they're charged in a joint criminal enterprise that you should be able to consider the evidence. We say it's also corroborative of other evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But is it not a traditional principle that evidence which is obtained outwith the presence of an accused person which he is not in a position to challenge since there's no saying whether Pavkovic will give evidence or not here, is it not the case that that sort of evidence can only be admissible against the person who makes the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know in my jurisdiction that is the general principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that when you have co-accused and when you have a statement from one, if his statement incriminates the other person, if we as the Prosecution are trying to introduce that evidence, we either have to have separate trials or we have to redact the statement in some fashion so, you know, it will make reference to an unknown person as opposed to the named co-accused, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In Scotland, we tend simply to tell juries to ignore it in relation to other accused, but some take the view that that has an effect of throwing a skunk into the jury box and then telling them to ignore the smell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Here, obviously, we can cope with the distinction, but it may be quite important I think, even in the 98 bis context, to be clear in our minds against whom a statement of this nature can be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- as I wonder -- I pose the question, I guess, does it make a difference if the statement is about a criminal act versus the existence of a particular governmental body? You know, if it's about a fact that is maybe neutral on its face as opposed to something that's clearly inculpatory, does that make a difference? Although I understand the argument that something that is seemingly neutral on its face a good lawyer can make a connection to another item and another item and another item and pretty soon it's incriminating that Jim was wearing a green shirt on Saturday night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that that argument depends on the evidence having no positive value in support of your case. I think the principle would extend that far, that something obtained outwith the presence of an accused and not open to challenge because it comes from a co-accused would not be admissible in support of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- can I continue on this for just another moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because I'm trying to think of the law in my own jurisdiction that -- may I consult for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm thinking about, for example, our Rule 92 quater which allows for written evidence of an unavailable witness because he's dead or because he can't appear because of physical or mental reasons, and that if we have written evidence from that witness we can offer it. And if the Trial Chamber finds that the statement was taken under circumstances or given under circumstances that tend to show it's reliable, that you can consider that evidence. But in our rule the definition -- in our rule in the Tribunal the definition of unavailability doesn't include a co-accused or someone who refuses to testify because his testimony might incriminate him. In my jurisdiction we have an exception to the rule against hearsay that we have, for example, a statement of an unavailable witness, either because he's refusing to testify because he might incriminate himself or because he's fled the jurisdiction, but he gave a statement at the time and at the time which he gave it the statement he gave was against his own interest, whether that's his criminal interest or pecuniary interest that gave it some indicia of reliability, it could be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, that's a fairly common exception nowadays, Mr. Hannis. I think it's a developing exception. I'm interested in the question of just how widespread is the practice of excluding this sort of evidence against an accused who can't challenge it. Indeed the very fact that we have the rule you've referred to, 92 quater, really works against your argument. The fact that that rule is necessary. Indeed, I'm quite certain that many domestic jurisdictions are far more lenient in their acceptance of the evidence of deceased witnesses, for example, than this jurisdiction is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, if there is anything more you want to say in reflexion on this, that can no doubt be said tomorrow and we can proceed with the rest of your submissions just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I will take a look at that and if I have something additional I will bring it to your attention tomorrow. But a couple of other documents we say reflect the existence of the Supreme Command or the continued existence and functioning of the Supreme Defence Council are found in Exhibit 1495 which was admitted on the 20th of March. It's from the 24th of May, 1999, and it makes reference to the Supreme Command undertaking a particular action, not the Supreme Command Staff, not the supreme commander. I think Exhibits 1480, 1480, and 1489, similarly have references to the Supreme Command. These are all after the 23rd of March, 1999. And I believe it's Exhibit 1481 dated the 9th of April, 1999, which is from General Ojdanic as head of the Supreme Command Staff and outlining detailed preparations for a possible invasion/conflict with NATO. And one of the things that it provides for I think it's at page 5 of the English it says: "At the level of the VSO," which is the Supreme Defence Council, "and the General Staff, organise communications and cryptographic communication with the president of the Republic of Serbia and the president of the Republic of Montenegro." Which would suggest that the Supreme Defence Council is continuing to exist. We say that the reference to "Supreme Command" is probably the wartime informal designation that's being used. In Exhibit P1996, staff -- the MUP staff minutes for a meeting on the 7th of May, 1999, attended by Mr. Sainovic and he spoke to the assembled MUP staff and told them about an order issued by the supreme commander, Slobodan Milosevic, which should be relayed to all police commanders as a task assigned by the Supreme Command. We also say, Your Honour, that logic dictates that if General Ojdanic is the head of the Supreme Command Staff, there must be some Supreme Command that that staff is serving. And, as I said, Mr. Stamp may have a couple of other items to bring to your attention when he discusses Mr. Milutinovic tomorrow. Your Honours, I would like to request if we could break early today. I know it's 20 minutes from time, but I'm -- frankly I'm not feeling very well now and I think I could do better if I could resume in the morning. I think there's a chance that we could spill into Monday with or without these 20 minutes, but I would make that request at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hannis. We have a similar length of day tomorrow. We have, I think, only half a day on Monday and we've arranged a similar length of day on Tuesday just in case. But the anticipation appears to be completion on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
